item.title: [a16z] Mark Cuban’s Plan to Make Healthcare Affordable
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最意外的观察：Mark Cuban 真正在卖的，不是药，是"信任的套利"

表面上看，Cost Plus Drugs 是一家药品公司。但如果你仔细听 Mark 的语言——"trust is still our primary product"——他真正在做的生意是信任的套利。

这里有一个几乎没人谈论的系统性真相：在一个被破坏的市场里，透明度本身是最稀缺的商品。15% 的毛利不是定价策略，它是信任的"票价"。消费者愿意为"我知道你没有骗我"支付溢价，哪怕这个"没骗我"的价格仍然低于被欺骗的价格。

更深层的洞察是：Mark 不是在和 CVS、United Health 竞争药品——他在和它们争夺消费者认知带宽中的"诚实槽位"。而这个槽位在整个经济体中几乎都是空的。这解释了一个诡异现象——为什么 UnitedHealth 的销售会在没有合同的情况下，谎称 Cost Plus 是他们网络的一部分：他们在偷用 Mark 的信任资本来掩盖自己的不信任赤字。这是品牌寄生，但寄生的不是 logo，而是道德权威。

二、跨领域连接：医疗 ASO 合同 = 加密货币的"智能合约悖论"倒影

Mark 讲到达拉斯市的 PBM 合同有 1335 页——他称之为"合同恐怖主义"。这里有一个让人不寒而栗的跨领域映射：

传统医疗合同是"反智能合约"。加密世界的智能合约承诺"代码即法律"——条款被压缩到可以在毫秒内验证执行。而医疗 ASO 合同走的是完全相反的路径：条款被故意膨胀到人类认知带宽无法处理的程度，使得"签字"和"理解"之间永久脱钩。

这揭示了一个被忽视的系统原理——复杂度本身是一种武器。它不是设计缺陷，是定价结构的一部分。1335 页不是律师的傲慢，是精心校准到人类注意力极限之上一寸的信息战。

而 Mark 的"用 AI 读合同"策略，本质上是在做什么？他在把 ASO 合同从"反智能合约"强制翻译回"智能合约"——用算力把语言复杂度压回到人类可处理的尺度。这是一个加密世界从未遇到过的问题的镜像解法：不是从代码走向法律，而是从法律的病理性膨胀反向走回代码。

同样的模式还藏在哪里？税法、劳动合同、服务条款、保险精算表、学区协议——所有"长度即保护"的领域都即将经历同样的 AI 压缩冲击。医疗只是第一张倒下的多米诺。

三、系统性预言：Cost Plus 的"Pod"是对工业革命的反向工程

大家都在听 Mark 说"20 亿美元 pod 业务"，但很少有人意识到他在描述什么。

工业革命的底层逻辑是：集中化 + 规模化 = 低成本。所以我们建了底特律、建了富士康、建了印度仿制药工厂。但 Mark 的制药 pod——$2000 万一个、拖车大小、每四小时切换药品、可以 daisy chain 组合——是对这个前提的根本性反叛。

他真正在做的是把"规模经济"重新定义为"配置经济"。规模经济说："越多越便宜。"配置经济说："越对越便宜。"一个研究医院为某个 N-of-one 病人订制药品的边际成本，比等待印度工厂改线便宜得多——如果 pod 就在隔壁房间。

这里的系统性真相是：AI 不是让制造业更智能，是让它更小、更近、更专。它的真正敌人不是劳动力成本，而是物流和合规延迟。pod 把两者同时折叠到接近零。

跨领域映射：这和 3D 打印、小型模块化核反应堆（SMR）、本地化食品生产系统是同一个浪潮。整个 20 世纪建立的"中心化生产 + 全球物流"范式，正在被 AI + 机器人 + 配置化重塑为"按需生产 + 零距离部署"——医药只是技术成熟度最先触顶的那一个。

Mark 真正的赌注不是药——是赌全球供应链的拓扑结构正在翻转。如果他赢了，印度仿制药工厂不是被更便宜的美国工厂打败，而是被 pod 的地理不可知性淘汰。工厂去找病人，而不是药去找病人。

四、一个藏在对话里的暗线：所有玩家都在"等一个契约时刻"

通读整个对话，有一个被 Mark 反复强调但没有被完整命名的现象——美国医疗系统的失败不是技术失败，是契约失败。

无论是 1335 页的 PBM 合同、EOB、ASO 的 835/837 文件、拒赔和清算、还是雇主对自身账单的无知——整个系统的病理学都发生在"签字那一刻"。AI 的 bot wars、provider 的 upcoding、支付方的 denial——这些都是契约签订后的军备竞赛后遗症。

Mark 的所有干预——cost plus wellness 开源合同、"把你的现有合同喂给 AI 问他们在哪里坑你"、公开州级 RFP——都指向同一个战略支点：把契约时刻变得对称。

这里的洞见是：整个美国医疗 4.5 万亿美元的无效支出，可能可以追溯到不到几千份被少数几家公司垄断了认知权的合同。如果你是风投，这意味着最高杠杆的医疗创业机会，不是做更好的医生、更好的 AI 诊断、更好的保险产品，而是做"合同反恐"——一个解析、比对、谈判支持的 AI 层，服役于那 160M 美国雇员。

这个市场从未被定义过。它的 TAM 可能大于所有数字健康公司加起来。

📝 转录文本

开场：医疗市场的根本失灵

We are not in an efficient healthcare market. The economics are broken.

One of the many ills of healthcare is that it completely lacks competitive dynamics. Just merely by the presence of plus drugs, you've actually forced change in [music] the incumbents.

United Health 3,000 plus subsidiaries, $150 billion in intercomp transfers annually. There's often times when they will increase premiums, increase deductibles, and at the same time force you into a relationship with a company they already own and you don't know they own them. The ultimate mission is to disrupt healthcare so that it's affordable again.

Is there like some area where you're like, why is no one building here? There's no better time to be an entrepreneur than right now. The biggest challenge and where AI, I think, is going to have the biggest impact is...

欢迎与引入

Well, Mark, welcome to the podcast. Thanks so much for joining.

Thanks for having me on, guys.

Julie, what has struck you about Mark's contributions in the space? What have you always found fascinating about what Mark's been up to with Cost Plus Drugs or and just in general, and why you invited him on to the show?

I mean, Mark, first of all, just had the courage to enter into the morass that is healthcare in a way that made such a splash — and that many, many people who, you know, also are in the privileged position that Mark is in to just have such a huge audience have been intimidated to do over many, many decades.

And so I've loved watching the market react to what Mark has done in healthcare. I think, you know, the one thing I know Mark — you and I have talked about this in the past — but healthcare is one of the industries where one of the many ills is that it completely lacks competitive dynamics and competitive forces, free market dynamics, all that kind of stuff.

And what's been fascinating to watch is just merely by the presence of Cost Plus Drugs as one example — and we'll talk about others that you've done too — but just merely by the presence of that entity and what you represent and what you're doing, you've actually forced change in the incumbents that otherwise, even with policy, even with all sorts of other forces, like never changed over the course of many, many decades.

Yeah, 'cause I don't get to see that stuff 'cause I don't talk to those guys.

影子网络效应：没有合同也在被引用

And then I think to your point, like even absent a contract, I think people are recognizing from the demand side of the market that they need to show that there is some pathway for people to get your product, right? And so perhaps even in the absence of a direct contract, I do hear people talking about your solution as part of their network.

Really, it truly does not surprise me when the big three or even the big six use our name as kind of a way to counter the request, you know, in the discussion of pricing — 'cuz they know that our prices are public, that anybody can take our API, and big companies that have half a brain are pulling that data on a daily basis, and they're saying, "You have to beat this price." And so I can see that.

But, you know, I've had at least one company and probably more that have said, "Oh yeah, it's, you know, pick one of the big three has told us that you're part of their network and we get your prices where you're cheaper," and we don't have an agreement at all with any of the big three.

业务版图巡览：四根支柱

Mark, let's zoom out and take stock about where you're at with the business. You launched in 2022 with a few dozen drugs. In April this year, you said you were up to roughly 4,000. You're getting into manufacturing, hospital contracts, potentially AI-based care. Why don't you take stock a little bit of where the business is?

1. Cost Plus Drugs（邮购）

I'll give you the rundown. So, we launched costplusdrugs.com — I mean January 19th of 2022. 111 medications, purely generic, and we didn't know what to expect at all. I went out and started talking about it and it immediately blew up, right?

And then our volumes there led the manufacturers to expand their portfolio with us and we were able to add additional manufacturers. So now, as you said, we have 4,000 SKUs give or take, and our business every week is up and to the right. So our biggest challenge is just keeping up with it. So that's segment number one.

2. Team Cuban Card（本地取药）

Then the obvious response to mail order is "well, I need to pick things up today." And so we created what's called the teamcubancard.com. I did not name it. And it's basically a discount card that allows you to go to any of the 17,000 pharmacies that have affiliated with us and pick up most of our drugs locally — because I'm a big believer in supporting independent pharmacy.

So we pay our affiliate pharmacies a $12 fill fee, which means that's going to make us more expensive for the lowest cost drugs — because if you have a $5 statin plus $12, you're going to get it cheaper somewhere else. But at the same time, if you really want to support your independent pharmacies, you can pick up the cheap drugs. But on the more expensive drugs, the specialty generics, the biosimilars, we're actually much cheaper. And for things like biosimilars and insulin and things that have cold shipping, it's actually cheaper to buy it and pick it up locally through our Team Cuban Card. So that's the second stool in what we offer.

3. 达拉斯制造与 Pod：把工厂塞进拖车

Third is cost plus marketplace. Well, before I get to cost plus marketplace, let me go back to our Dallas manufacturing.

A big part of — Alex, my co-founder, Dr. Oxmanski — his original cold email to me was he wanted to manufacture drugs that are generic drugs that are on the FDA short supply list, because there are pediatric cancer drugs, there are things that are widely used in hospitals — penicillin, oxytocin, epinephrine — this long list of drugs.

And we were able to use AI and robotics to shrink what would have been a football field or more into 5,000 square feet. And not only that, but we were able to turn drugs every four hours. So we can make a six-month supply, turn the line, and then go to the next drug. And we sell those products to hospitals and clinics.

An extension of that — because we've been doing that, we've been working on that five years ago — we've been able to take those same robotics and AI and shrink it into a manufacturing plant, if you will, the size of a tractor trailer. And we call those pods. And those pods can be used for anything and shipped anywhere.

The government was our first customer. We've shipped the first one here recently where we just got an order for a second, and they told us there's more behind that — because if there's an ecological disaster, we can send it to FEMA (if FEMA's around). If there is a weather disaster, military disaster, God forbid, we can ship them there and configure them to make any specific type of drug.

So we can configure a pod for sterile injectables — multiple pods can be daisy-chained together so we can scale, and/or you can have one being a sterile room and another doing the tablet work for generics. I'm not the expert on this; Alex can go into this in precise detail.

But the thing I'm most proud of — and actually Stat News just wrote a story on this yesterday or the day before — is that we can take these pods and configure them to do N-of-one therapies, so that we can ship the pod to a research hospital. These pods cost about $20 million. Ship it to a research hospital, and if they specialize in any types of therapies for those people that are in the N-of-one category, they can make it and iterate very quickly there. And then now we're doing these ASO drugs — and don't ask me what ASO stands for because I can't pronounce it — out of our first manufacturing facility in Dallas. So that's part two.

4. Cost Plus Marketplace

From that manufacturing, we created costplusmarketplace.com. And Cost Plus Marketplace takes those sterile injectables we make, and others that we source from other providers or other manufacturers, and we sell them at a cost-plus-10 or cost-plus-12 to clinics, hospitals, providers — whoever wants to buy them at the cheapest price. And we literally can save hospitals millions of dollars a year.

But our biggest challenge there is we convince the CEOs, but we can't always convince the purchasing people to do it.

5. 直接合同与开源契约：Cost Plus Wellness

And then finally, because of my own experiences as a self-insured employer, and going around and talking to hospital CEOs and CFOs and learning their relationship with the big carriers, the big vertically integrated carriers, and all the things they like and dislike — mostly dislike — I went to them and said:

"Look, I know you hate the delays, the denies, the pre-auths, the late pays, the clawbacks, the fact that the carrier plans keep on increasing deductibles, turning the providers into subprime lenders because they have to collect the deductibles before they can offer the care, or before they can get access to the insurance money.

Knowing all these things, I'd like to work out a direct contract, but I want two things. I'm going to tell you what I'm going to give you in exchange for those two things.

One, I'm going to trust the doctor. Unless it's something crazy, trust the doctor. So you're not going to need a pre-auth. There aren't going to be denials. Now, we had somebody who had Munchausen's disease that required a denial — but other than that, if it's something crazy. I'm going to pay the price that we contract for on time. I'm going to take responsibility for the patient out of pocket. Either I'll pay it, or I'll take the credit risk for the patient itself. So you're not a subprime lender.

And in exchange for all that, I want two things. I want a better price, because your associated administration and overhead and doctor time is much less, your yield's going to be higher. And I want the ability to take the contract we signed — this direct contract between us — and publish it on costpluswellness.com, so it can act as open source for all of these contracts, so that any employer can use them and any provider can post their contract. And even if you don't want to post or use, you can use them as templates in your own negotiations."

雇主赞助保险的大替换周期

Well, I love the last piece, Mark, because I think that was the genesis of our thread back and forth when I published a piece a few weeks ago on what I'm calling the great replacement cycle of health plans.

You're going to use this software that I require, because nobody's going to give away that IP for free." And that creates a lot more problems.

I think part of the underpinning that a lot of AI entrepreneurs have is that — going back to Aaron, "information wants to be free" — the information may want to be free, but the person who owns the IP feels differently. And so that's going to change how we interact with models.

We can argue about frontends that choose which model is least expensive to answer the question, but we haven't had the discussion on where we find the IP that's needed to either train that model, post-train that model, RAG that model, whatever it may be — if that person isn't making it available, but it's absolutely required.

Does that make sense to you guys? Or do you guys think I'm an idiot?

未来需要更多医生而非更少

You know, I think it's really interesting because it also brings up the point of like, what is the role of the doctor in the future? Number one, I agree — actually, I think we're going to need more doctors in the future, because as care advice becomes more abundant, more people are going to demand healthcare, actual real-life healthcare services. And so we're going to find we actually need more doctors.

And there's something to be said about what you're describing as — the role of the doctor today is very rote. It's kind of like these are the tasks you got to do, these quality measures. You barely need to use your brain, honestly, for a lot of the things that doctors are asked to do in the traditional healthcare setting. And what you're describing is like, what if the paradigm moves towards physicians are actually more physician-scientists? Like it's actually their job is to take the bleeding edge of information that we may not know at population scale yet, but on an individual basis they're at the tip of the spear of collecting novel data, generating novel insights about how people are reacting.

Novel data — by definition, stimulating job description to me.

Yes.

Yes. Because by definition — you're exactly right. Novel data equals person.

Mhm. Exactly. And with data —

纵向监测与可穿戴设备

We're going to have longitudinal monitoring. Like the blood pressure is the one that we always talk about, where it's kind of the same principle as what you're saying. The fact that we take our blood pressure once a year is kind of ridiculous because it changes.

Not me.

I got this s*** right here.

You're — yeah, [laughter] you're cutting edge.

And soon we're going to have wearables that are just measuring it in real time, like every single day. And you'll have a much more precise understanding of how you're responding to different therapeutic interventions, and even diet and exercise, and all that kind of stuff.

新职业：AI 翻译员

And that's going to — you bring up a good point, Julie — in terms of novel information. And that's everybody, in terms of finding jobs. You're going to need AI translators for people who may not keep up with these things. Regular people that are in wherever in this country or in the world who just want to live their abundance life, whatever that may be. And you're going to need people who are going to be the translators for what's novel about this circumstance or this individual, and how do you make it valid to AI and the output of the AI valid to the novel to the individual.

That's going to be a job, and it's going to be very difficult to extract everything from an individual that the AI is going to need. And you're going to need to have a person there to do it. Maybe somebody envisions a humanoid robot that is going to ask you those questions, and somebody's going to be comfortable. I don't think that's going to happen.

关于 EHR：Epic 的世界

By the way, Mark, I don't think I've ever heard you talk about another set of entrenched incumbents, which is the EHR companies. What's your theory of the case there — how that market changes or evolves or doesn't in the age of AI, and what that looks like in the next few years?

Honestly, I don't know. The EHR is dominated by Epic, and it's their world. And so I've just kind of deferred to them and tried to stick where I can have an impact — because we partner with them. We think offering pricing (particularly pharmaceutical pricing) at the point of script, where the doctor is there offering them different options, is a —

Part of that new announcement that they just made about the —

Yeah, exactly. With Epic and Amazon, etc. So I think that's a big plus, and I think that's needed. But in terms of their actual business and where it's disruptable, I'm not really the one qualified for that.

Okay. My problem, by the way, with that announcement was that they announced it and then they said it's not going to be available till May of next year, and I was like, why take so long?

I had nothing to do with that. [laughter]

That's typical in this industry, right?

GDP、生产力与"疾病护理"vs"健康护理"

Do you guys think that in 10 years, healthcare is still going to be a fifth or a sixth of whatever it is now of GDP? And is there kind of this sort of terminal state where there's just way more demand than we can supply, and just as it gets easier, as it gets more efficient, we're still — and as GDP grows even 5% a year, hopefully — at some point our demand is still going to cap at 1/5 of the economy?

I do.

Yeah. But the value that we get out of that spend should be —

Well, the value you get out of the people will increase.

Yeah.

Because they'll be healthier.

Yeah.

So there's a difference when it's healthcare — when it's sick care, as a lot of people refer to — versus when it's keeping people healthy, and they're more productive, and there's less downtime, and they're smarter because it's easier to learn, etc.

So I think we'll get greater productivity that'll more than account for it, which we don't get now.

假如 Mark 是总统：五点医疗政策

Zooming out a bit, Mark, we have a mutual friend who's a very prominent pollster — I won't out him here — but he believes, or he's done some work to indicate, that if you ever ran for office, he thinks you could win. Of course, you've said you'll never run. So, speaking hypothetically now: if you were president or if you were advising the next president, I'm curious how you would think about what is the leverage to most address our healthcare challenges, and then I want to hear your broader policy positions.

It's really easy. It's the same thing I tell states that I've testified for.

One, make all contracts with anybody who takes taxpayer money public. No redactions. Because the minute that happens, you start to have an efficient market and the costs go down.

Two, make it so that anybody who can find a better price for less than their current out-of-pocket with their plan, make it apply to their deductible. Allow it to apply to their deductible. Eight states do that at some level already.

Three, for nonprofit hospitals, require them to publish their entire general ledger down to each detailed entry and all their procurement receipts and requirements — so that everybody gets to see it. It's our money. We're the taxpayers.

Four, instead of current insurance plans the way we have them — 72% of those big carriers' revenue comes from taxpayers. They don't take risk anymore. They offload it. Everything's an arbitrage for them.

So, knowing that, we also have to consider that the one debt we never pay off till the day we die is our insurance premiums. Think about that — whether it's Medicare, unless you're on Medicaid, you are paying till the day you expire. And when you need it, you have to fight for it in the current system, and probably foreseeable systems.

一个替代方案：个人医疗储蓄 + 联邦贷款担保 + 止损

To me, if we were able to create a program where you just deposited what would be — let's just say how much you'd pay for a premium under an ACA silver plan in your state — and we just went and did a deal with the bank and said: "Okay, in Texas for a family of five it's $2,100 at your income, right? So you just keep on depositing $2,100 and it accrues and you own it, but it has to be deposited if you want to participate in this program."

And then if you have a medical incident or pharmaceutical incident — you can take that money. If it's not enough, we've worked out a deal with the bank where two things happen:

One, the bank will loan you money up until a point where stop-loss kicks in — which means we're going to take part of that money you deposit and use it for stop-loss coverage.

Two, the federal government or the state is going to guarantee that loan to you, so that the provider is not out, and we're still going to deduct it from your payroll so that you pay it back.

And if you're lucky and you never have an incident, you get to save all that money when you turn 65 and go on Medicare — you just get all that money and all the accrued interest.

Because if you think about it, the federal government will cover or guarantee your student loans. They'll guarantee SBA loans. They'll guarantee home loans or give you a down payment, right?

Like our internet —

Third-world country.

They'll guarantee all these things, even agricultural things. But the most important thing — covering our healthcare, good luck. You know, you're in a bad accident, good luck to you, and we'll maybe push it off to the hospitals. They have to take you in.

So I would create a plan that says: you have to deposit this money. The bank will have a guarantee just like a mortgage, whatever. We'll loan you this money, and then we'll have federal stop-loss programs above some amount — $40,000, whatever it may be. Now, all of a sudden, bye-bye insurance companies. Now, all of a sudden, you're not fighting back, because it's your money to spend as you choose.

Now, we'll have to set thresholds on where and how you could spend it, so you don't just go give it to your cousin Billy who said he's going to fix your broken toe. But within those constraints, I think now all of a sudden we have a better system. So that's what I would do if I was advising in terms of healthcare.

给 AI 行业的营销建议

What about — one of your gifts is storytelling and marketing more generally. What about the AI industry? AI is uniquely unpopular in the US. If you were advising OpenAI, if you were advising Anthropic, on how to change those numbers — and then there's the whole data center saga. I'm curious what your advice would be to the broader AI industry.

I've had these conversations with them, and I told them they're idiots. Because what controls how pretty much everybody in this country thinks right now? Social media algorithms.

Literally, I was having a conversation with a 23-year-old friend that I work with, and we're talking politics — we're discussing who we voted for yesterday, and how and why. And I said, "What about your friends, the other 23-24 year olds?" And they said that their friends didn't even know (living in Texas) didn't even know who Ken Paxton or James Terico were. Which is insane in my mind, but it reinforces the fact that you get more of what you seek via algorithms.

And if you really have the best AI, you should be able to not only reverse-engineer those algorithms, but put together a marketing program — because you sure tell everybody you can do marketing programs through your bots, or DOT or whatever — and really start marketing there. Because this applies to politics, it applies to AI, it applies to everything in this country, the divisiveness.

We all have our unique AI feed in the social media platforms we use, and those platforms don't give a f*** what it feeds you within some minimal constraints. And so everybody looks at the world differently.

The days — particularly for younger people — of thinking "just buy more ads and ruin our football games and our basketball games and everything's fine" — maybe older people vote more, and that's maybe why — but it's useless when you're trying to change hearts and minds about AI specifically. Even though the irony of it all is that it's the AI behind the algorithms that's ruining everything.

But as long as Section 230 is there, we are where we are. And as long as — unless we take an Australia-type approach or some states-type approach of 16-and-under — my advice to them specifically was: you need to use your AI to segment everything and figure out the best way to put together marketing, promotion, and however else you want to do it. Do it like the Russians do it. It doesn't matter, right? Because that's what's at stake for you.

But people — data-center hate is just a proxy for not being able to understand AI. And not knowing all the pieces there. And I don't blame people at all. Just like employers have been really dumb with their healthcare benefits, a lot of communities have been really dumb with the deals they've negotiated for data centers — they've fallen for the contractual terrorism in a lot of cases.

But educating them about social media, and educating our legislators and whoever's president about social media, because I don't think they truly understand the impact that we don't all read the same newspaper, the same magazines, look at the same websites, watch the same news shows. We all have our own unique TikTok feed.

Your feed is not like mine. The best way to find out about your kids is to just look at their social media feed. My 17-year-old son — it's basketball, basketball, basketball. Now I'm starting to see a little bit of politics pop up, but then hot girl, hot girl, hot girl, basketball, basketball, car, car. And I'm like, okay, typical 17-year-old guy, right?

But until the big frontier models understand completely that they have to figure out how to become part of everybody's feed — they're going to be putting out all these position papers that are useless.

创业的空白地带：所有地方

No, I mean, Mark, we agree with you that this is like the best time to be alive and an entrepreneur. And so many things that again were intractable historically are now all of a sudden addressable. Is there an area of the market — and you meet a lot of entrepreneurs and see people building in all sorts of areas of the world — is there like some area where you're like, "Why is no one building here?" that you think is still a whitespace opportunity for entrepreneurs?

两种公司，两种人

All of them. Seriously. When I go talk to kids, I always tell them: there's going to be two types of companies — those who are great at AI, and those who have gone out of business.

And if you take the time to learn — then there's two types of people and how they use AI: those who use AI to learn anything, and those who use AI so they don't have to learn anything.

And if you're one of those people who uses AI so that you can learn anything, and you realize what type of companies and problems aren't being solved by AI — don't be shy to just talk to your AI.

And I say this not just to kids — to 50-year-old, 60, 70-year-old entrepreneurs. The biggest challenge right now with people, entrepreneurs using AI, is the comfort level of talking to your AI — whether it's by voice or typing, whatever it is — because there's still a lot of hesitancy.

Just like back in the day, those first spreadsheets, people still had their 10-key adding machine, and they would check it to make sure the spreadsheets were right. You still do have to check the output, but you have the opportunity to take the output of Grok and put it into ChatGPT. And the output of — like when I go through all these contracts I was telling you about, I start with one and say, "Hey, one of your peers came out and said this about this contract. What do you think?" And spend a couple hours.

That's all. Young entrepreneurs — so when you ask me, is there one thing? I truly believe it's everything. Everything will change. This is the greatest transitional technology we have ever seen, and I've been around for all of them. And this blows them all away.

The hardest part is just going for it. And that's where Silicon Valley, and kids from the Bay Area, I think, have a little bit of an advantage — because they see their parents and friends and the culture there as "little go." But I think the rest of the country and the rest of the world, once they get that confidence level, you're going to start to see businesses we never imagined pop up — because we're not seeing that yet.

We're not seeing companies where it's like, "Oh, what is that? Why are they doing that? What is the opportunity there?" And then they realized it before we did, right? It's kind of like Napster — first like, "Whoa, what was that?"

So I think the biggest thing to focus on if you're looking for something is: ask anything. I do it all the time. It's just like, "What do you think about this? What do you think about this? What do you think about this?"

I've held phones up next to each other and taken the output and had them have a conversation with each other so I could listen in. Don't be shy about using AI in things that feel really uncomfortable and weird — because that uncomfortableness is probably the path to something that is groundbreaking and game-changing.

结束

That's a great note to wrap on. Mark, thank you so much for coming on the podcast.

It was fun. Thanks, guys. Thanks, Julie. Thanks, Eric.

item.description:
## 一、最意外的观察：Mark Cuban 真正在卖的，不是药，是"信任的套利"
表面上看，Cost Plus Drugs 是一家药品公司。但如果你仔细听 Mark 的语言——"trust is still our primary product"——他真正在做的生意是**信任的套利**。
这里有一个几乎没人谈论的系统性真相：**在一个被破坏的市场里，透明度本身是最稀缺的商品**。15% 的毛利不是定价策略，它是信任的"票价"。消费者愿意为"我知道你没有骗我"支付溢价，哪怕这个"没骗我"的价格仍然低于被欺骗的价格。
更深层的洞察是：Mark 不是在和 CVS、United Health 竞争药品——他在和它们**争夺消费者认知带宽中的"诚实槽位"**。而这个槽位在整个经济体中几乎都是空的。这解释了一个诡异现象——为什么 UnitedHealth 的销售会在没有合同的情况下，谎称 Cost Plus 是他们网络的一部分：**他们在偷用 Mark 的信任资本来掩盖自己的不信任赤字**。这是品牌寄生，但寄生的不是 logo，而是道德权威。

item.title: [Lex Clips] Mathematician explains Navier-Stokes equations | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个颠覆性的观察：Navier-Stokes 其实不是"流体方程"，而是任何有记忆、有惯性、受约束的分布式系统的通用语法

听 Lex 的解释，大多数人会把注意力放在"流体"二字上。但真正令人震撼的是：如果你把这段描述里的"velocity field"替换成"情绪场"、"注意力场"、"资金流向场"、"神经元激活场"——方程的骨架几乎不需要改动。这不是比喻，而是数学同构。

  • 速度场 = 系统在每个点的"倾向性"
  • 压强 = 全局约束（守恒律的"看不见的手"）
  • 动量 = 历史的持续性（为什么系统不能瞬间转向）
  • 粘性 = 内部摩擦（为什么蜂蜜难搅、为什么大型组织难改革）
  • 外力 = 来自系统外的能量注入（加热、重力——或：政策、热点、情绪冲击）

这意味着社交网络的"信息湍流"、金融市场的"恐慌传播"、甚至大语言模型内部 token 之间的"注意力漩涡"，本质上都在跑一个变形的 Navier-Stokes。 这就是为什么 2022 年之后 AI 领域爆发的 Flow Matching、Rectified Flow、Diffusion Models 的核心词汇全都来自流体力学——不是借用术语，是认领了同一个数学现实。

跨领域连接：龙卷风的低压核心 = 爆款内容的"注意力黑洞" = Transformer 的 attention sink

Lex 顺口一句"the core of a tornado is low pressure"藏着一个你可能从未注意的系统性真相：所有自组织的漩涡，中心都是"空的"。

  • 龙卷风中心：气压最低，所以周围的空气被"吸"进来旋转
  • 爆款短视频：内容本身往往极简甚至"空洞"（一个表情、一句口号），但正因如此，人们才能向其投射自己的意义，形成传播漩涡
  • Transformer 大模型里的 "attention sink"（2023 年才被广泛发现）：模型会把大量注意力"倾倒"到第一个 token 这种语义空洞的位置，否则整个注意力分布会崩溃
  • 组织里的"沉默领导者"：话最少的那个人往往聚集最多的信息流

一个让人起鸡皮疙瘩的猜想：是不是所有的旋转结构，都必须有一个"低势能"的核心才能稳定存在？压强的高低差驱动流动——那么在社会系统里，驱动人群聚集的从来不是"中心的实体"，而是中心的"缺失"。流体力学可能是我们理解"为什么大人物往往轮廓模糊"的最严格的学科。

隐藏的系统性真相：粘性 ≠ 阻碍，而是系统能够"记住"自己的唯一方式

人们总把粘性（viscosity）理解为"摩擦力"、"阻力"——负面的、拖后腿的东西。蜂蜜不如水好用，水不如空气轻盈。但从动力系统的视角看，没有粘性的 Navier-Stokes 方程（即 Euler 方程）在数学上会在有限时间内爆炸——速度场会在某点变成无穷大，整个系统失去意义。

换句话说：粘性不是让系统变慢的东西，而是让系统能够存在的东西。

这个洞见可以直接搬到任何系统： - 一个没有任何"组织惯性"的公司，不是敏捷，是会在压力下瞬间崩解 - 一个完全没有情绪延迟的人，不是理性，是失去自我连续性的病态 - 一个没有正则化（regularization，数学上就是加一个粘性项）的神经网络，不会学习，只会在训练数据上爆炸性过拟合

真正的"啊哈时刻"在这里：Navier-Stokes 千禧年难题之所以悬而未决（我们至今不知道三维解是否永远光滑），本质上是在问一个关于所有复杂系统的终极问题——"内部摩擦（粘性）是否足以永远阻止集中性崩溃？" 这个问题在气候、在大脑、在社会、在 AI 训练中反复出现，形式不同，灵魂相同。

你问的从来不只是一个方程。你问的是：分布式系统的记忆、约束与崩溃的边界，到底在哪里。

📝 转录文本

The Building Block: A Velocity Field

What are the different components of the Navier-Stokes equation? Can you — if you — can you dig in? Like, what does it take to describe fluid?

Yeah. So very, very basic: a fluid moves, and it moves differently in different places and at different points in time. And so the kind of basic building block of a fluid is the velocity field. So at every point in space, there is a velocity vector that tells you how that fluid is moving. You know, maybe it's really fast here and slow here, and it creates a vortex.

When Velocity Changes Rapidly: Vortices and Pressure

Um, and it gets more interesting when the fluid velocity changes a lot over space. So like a tornado is a very rapidly changing fluid velocity field in both space and time.

There's pressures that are involved. So again, like the core of a tornado is low pressure. So pressures are, um, kind of forcing this velocity field and causing it to move in the way it does. That's the building block — a velocity field and its pressures.

How the Field Evolves: Momentum, Viscosity, External Forces

And then the equations tell you how that velocity changes in time and in space according to kind of its own momentum. So fluid has momentum to carry itself — that's, you know, gusts of wind.

It has internal friction and resistance. That's viscosity. So honey has more internal resistance than water, has more internal resistance than air.

Um, and then all of the external forces like heating and pressure and gravity and things like that. So each of those can be quantified as a term in this, this larger Navier-Stokes equation.

item.title: [Sequoia Capital] European Defense Sovereignty Starts in the Factory: Stark’s Uwe Horstmann and Johannes Schaback
item.dc:creator: Sequoia Capital
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个让人意外的观察：这家公司其实不是在卖武器，而是在卖"工程摩擦力的消失"

读完整个访谈，表面上 Stark 做的是打击无人机、海上无人系统、电子战。但如果你把访谈里真正被反复强调的词剔出来——"洗衣机"、"木头盒子"、"三班倒"、"合同设计"、"士官的鼠标点击"、"手套下的触控"——你会发现他们真正在兜售的不是"杀伤能力"，而是把国防工业那套根深蒂固的"庄严缓慢"替换成消费电子的"轻盈快速"。

一台能摧毁坦克的武器被工程师骄傲地形容为"复杂度跟洗衣机差不多"——这句话放在冷战军工复合体的话术里是亵渎，放在今天却是最高褒奖。他们贩卖的其实是抽象层的下沉：把过去只有洛克希德-马丁、Thales 这类巨头能聚合的"航空级工程"，拉到了白色家电的制造曲线上。真正的产品不是无人机，而是"washing-machine-ification of weapons"。

跨领域连接：Stark 的"士兵中心主义" ≈ 丰田的"现场主义" + Figma 的"用户同席开发"

Uve 说得很直白：传统军工把采购决策者（将军）当客户，而他们把使用者（士官、列兵）当客户。这个结构性的转变其实在三个完全不同的领域都反复发生过：

  • 制造业：丰田的 genchi genbutsu（现地现物）——工程师必须到车间地板上，而不是在图纸上做决定。
  • SaaS：Figma 彻底颠覆了 Adobe，不是因为它功能更强，而是因为它把"签合同的 CTO"和"每天用软件的设计师"的决策权重倒过来了。
  • 医疗器械：直觉外科（Intuitive Surgical）早期之所以能撬动达芬奇机器人，是因为它绕开了医院采购委员会，让主刀医生自己上手。

真正让人意外的洞察在这里：当"使用者 ≠ 决策者"的鸿沟越大，颠覆空间就越大。军队是地球上这个鸿沟最大的组织（一个 60 岁的四星将军决定一个 23 岁下士手里的触摸屏布局），所以这里不是"也可以用启动思维做"，而是结构上注定了必然被颠覆——只是过去没人敢碰。换句话说，Stark 看起来是在赌欧洲地缘政治，其实是在赌一个比战争更稳定的规律：客户-用户错位越严重的市场，颠覆的赔率越高。

隐藏的系统性真相：欧洲的"迟缓"这次成了防御性优势

有一个被很多人忽略的反直觉事实在访谈里一闪而过——Uve 说"欧洲变革不是因为出现了一位魅力型领袖让大家跟我走，欧洲是基于'好吧看来我们必须这么做了'才改变。"

一般叙事会把这解读为"欧洲又慢又官僚"。但他紧接着的那半句才是关键："正因如此，这些改变可能更持久。"

这是一个绝妙的系统性洞察：由危机驱动的、结构性被迫的、集体默认的改变，比由愿景驱动的、英雄主义式的、个人号召的改变更难逆转。 因为前者没有可以撤回的"主角"。

类比一下： - 美国的国防创新常常绑在某任国防部长、某位总统、某个 SPAC 周期上——容易随政治翻盘。 - 欧洲的改变一旦发生，是嵌在 27 国采购指令、BAFIN 条例、NATO 认证流程里的——反而更难开倒车。

所以 Stark 真正押注的，不是"欧洲这次终于醒了"，而是欧洲一旦醒了就睡不回去。这跟软件行业里一个古老的现象完全同构：一旦一个公司迁移到 Kubernetes，无论后悔不后悔，它都迁不回去了。路径依赖在制度层面产生的粘性，往往比在技术层面更强。

一个被低估的信号：Johannes 想重新设计的不是武器，而是"合同"

当 Pat 问"下一个最难的问题是什么"，Johannes 回答的既不是续航、也不是 AI 模型精度，而是——合同的结构设计。他想要的是一种类似"云服务突发容量"（surge capacity）的国防合同：平时少量库存，战时按需秒级扩产。

这才是整个访谈最有预言性的一句话。因为它意味着：未来真正的威慑力不是你有多少无人机，而是你能否在 72 小时内把每月 1 万台扩到每月 10 万台。这把威慑的"状态变量"从存量（库存）转成了流量（制造弹性）——跟亚马逊 AWS 当年把"你有多少服务器"重新定义为"你能按需拉起多少服务器"是同一个认知革命。

当国防工业开始用 AWS 式的合同思维签约时，整个西方军工复合体就彻底变样了。而这个暗号，Stark 已经悄悄在埋了。

开场：欧洲必须对自己负责

Uwe： I think what came together is obviously an understanding in Europe that Europe needs to take more responsibility for its own defense. You know, that is of course something that the US have told us repeatedly. Um, and they're right. You know, Europe has to step up and needs to be able to defend itself because that is our way of continuing to live in peace. It's deterrence, right?

[music]

主持人： My partner Luchiano and I are here with Uwe and Johannes, the co-founders of Stark, a neoprime serving the European defense community. Gentlemen, thank you for joining us.

Uwe & Johannes： Thank you so much for having us. Thank you.

一、18 个月内拿下数十亿美元合同：到底做对了什么？

主持人： All right, to get things started, you guys landed billions of dollars of contracts within 18 months of starting the company, which I believe is unheard of in the defense business. What did you do, right? How did that happen?

Uwe： So, obviously, you know, this is something that we like to claim as a big success, but it's also probably a moment that is just optimistic for all of us because something has changed beyond just what we built in our company and we're moving in the right direction.

I think in Europe what we did specifically is four things:

  1. We did innovation really close to the battlefield — really being integrated with units and soldiers who actually use the systems.
  2. Be venture first thanks to Sequoia and others, which basically means we fund the innovation, kind of the product development, ourselves. We don't rely on some government R&D spending.
  3. We focus on designing the products in a way that they become really usable and mass deployable — so beyond pure innovation use cases all the way to certification, validation, safety of the systems. Really usable for NATO forces.
  4. We designed the products clearly thinking industrial scaling from the get-go — how can we make sure that those are not only a few exquisite systems that stand around somewhere, but how can we make sure that factories part of the weapon production is deterrence.

二、如何真正接近战场？

主持人： Now, let me ask you on point number one. Close to the battlefield — I'm guessing that most military units would not let a couple of random guys traipse into their units and understand their needs. How is it that you gained access to the battlefield so early in the life of the company?

Uwe： We do that with a large presence in Ukraine. So we have a large team in Ukraine and we integrate in those units quite extensively. We also do work with the European forces. So there are more and more formats where that thing is enabled — you can connect with the soldiers, you can show up with them, you can go to the battleground and the testing grounds, the training grounds. That's where you get the best feedback.

That is the most important input factor for us. The capital we can get — again, thanks to Sequoia and other people — but what we really need is that input of the customer, which is not necessarily the buyer. The buyer is probably some high-level official, but the customer oftentimes is a relatively simple soldier on an operational tactical level. We need their input. That's more important to us than anything else.

三、从木箱到心智负荷：产品是什么

主持人： Well, and just to level set on what you guys do — what is it you heard from those customers and what's the product that you've now given them in response?

Uwe： So at any point in time, we probably run 10 to 15 different programs almost like a venture-like innovation portfolio. The one at the moment is what you would probably call a strike drone. It's actually a munition, but it's a weapon system that is very much software and AI driven. It's relatively inexpensive compared to what other weapon systems are out there. And we got a lot of great feedback on the usability.

We only begin to understand: what does it do to the mental load of a soldier who is supposed to operate those unmanned swarms? How exactly does that work? How should the box be created? Should it be wood? Should it be plastics? How do we visualize a swarm on a small screen so that a soldier can operate it?

塑料盒 vs. 木盒：实验室与前线的鸿沟

主持人： Earlier you had this interesting anecdote about plastic versus wood on the boxes that go into the field. Can you share that anecdote because I think that really illustrates kind of the difference between the lab and the field.

Uwe： 1,000%. Because you often have those great ideas how this product should be, and you came up with the idea on a whiteboard, and then you put it in front of the users, the soldiers using it in the field — either in real battle or in trainings and simulations — and sometimes it's very very different.

So for example, we show up with this beautiful plastic box that is light to carry, and they just sort of look at us like: "What do we do with this? Why don't you give us wood? Because wood at least we can put in the fire and it keeps us warm in the winter." Like, didn't think about that. [laughter]

And there's many anecdotes like that. The feedback is so valuable. So traditionally you would say the most important soldiers in the product development and the procurement are the generals who tell you that's where the big big budgets are and you should do this and that. And for us, we always like to say, the staff sergeants, the enlisted personnel who then actually use those systems, are maybe even more important to us. Because like in a true startup spirit, you want to be close to the customer. You want to develop for that customer. The customer for us — yes, it's the buyer, but it's also the user. And those are not the same people in a military situation.

We're just beginning, for example, to understand: if you think about a drone swarm that you are now controlling, how exactly do you do that? Do you have a mouse? Do you have a keyboard? Do you have a touchpad? How does it work when you wear gloves? What clicks are okay? Where do you need to be really precise? What is the mental load? How much information can I process at the same time? We're only beginning to understand.

把士兵当作客户

Uwe： If you treat soldiers — they are used to industry just showing up and dumping stuff on them and saying, "Here, this is the best thing. If you have issues with it, it's because you didn't understand it." You really need to change it around. You need to treat them as your customer. The most valuable thing they can give to you is their time and their feedback. And sometimes we show up and they say, "You know what? This is absolute shit." But you can really win trust by saying, "Tell us how exactly," and [laughter] we'll show up again tomorrow or the day after tomorrow — we create a new version and we'll be a bit, little bit less tomorrow. And that goes a long way.

Some of the things that make me the proudest of this company is we gained lots of minds and hearts in the community by people saying, "You know what, those guys, they approach it from the right perspective. They have a soldier-centric view and they really want to build a product that's good for us."

It's quite obvious for startup people — probably everybody who sits here says, "Yeah, we want to build for the customer, the customer needs to be happy, Net Promoter Score, retention, NRR and ARR growth." And for us, the translation to that is: listen to the soldiers, build with them, build for them, and hopefully good things will happen on the procurement side as well.

四、欧洲为何在此刻出现"neoprime"的机会？

主持人： Can we take a step back? You mentioned that there is a favorable moment in Europe right now for building defense companies. And Uwe, you and I have known each other for a long time. We started as venture capitalists in Europe and you saw the opportunity in defense before other people. You were investing in defense way before it was obvious, I would say. And you also have a background in the military yourself. Can you tell us a little bit firstly about what came together in Europe and why there is this opportunity to build a new neoprime today?

Uwe： I think what came together is obviously an understanding in Europe that Europe needs to take more responsibility for its own defense. That is of course something that the US have told us repeatedly, and they're right. Europe has to step up and needs to be able to defend itself because that is our way of continuing to live in peace. It's deterrence, right?

We probably understand now that the world is unfortunately probably not as default peaceful as it ideally would be, but it needs to be defended. And the only way we can be safe is by deterring a potential attacker. So that understanding has really materialized in people's minds.

And it came together with a point where people also understand something's happening on the battlefield. New technologies emerge. It's software-driven, AI-driven, it's relatively inexpensive to produce. It is small-scale. And those two points came together, and we give a lot of credit to the Germans and other governments who also understood: well, if that's the case, we should (a) procure those solutions where the capabilities that we have are lacking or there's a gap, and (b) we also need to change the process of how we procure, because you don't procure a drone like you procure a battleship. It's just different.

So that did come together and that was probably the starting point for us, coinciding with the founding of the company, saying: okay, now we need to lean in. This is going to be one of those moments where in a few years we probably will ask ourselves, "what did we do during that time?" And for me, as you kind of mentioned my biography, things really came together — two big streams: an interest in military and security, international relations, things like that, and then the technology part. So it was quite a clear moment for me to say: okay, I need to step in.

采购流程的变化是否可持续？

主持人： Do you think that the procurement process changes are sustainable, or do you think this is a moment in time for Europe, for Germany and other European countries?

Uwe： I think they are sustainable. Changes like that in Europe, they don't happen because there is a charismatic leader who says, "You know, we need to change, this is the way, follow me, here's a great narrative." That's not how Europe works. Europe works based on, "Well, I guess we kind of have to do it now. It's reality." [laughter]

And the positive side of that would be: hopefully changes are more lasting because they are based on actual structural fundamental changes. Now we are in a new world. And that's what gives me hope that we change the procurement processes — that took years — to months. And that includes the certification, which is a big big part of what we do. It's a very boring topic in a way, but it's very very important. I think those changes are there to last because the real learning from the Ukraine-Russia war is probably not drones, no drones — it is about an innovation ecosystem that is the actual wonder weapon.

You know, we always like to read on the internet, "what new weapon system, how awesome is it?" That doesn't really matter. The whole point is: how do we as Western society set up ourselves so that we can continuously innovate in defense with all the different ingredients? We already talked about the input from fighting soldiers. There's a talent aspect of it — our smartest minds should be willing to work in defense. There's a capital aspect to it, and all that stuff. I think that is there to last. I'm quite hopeful about it.

五、2 岁的公司凭什么打赢 70 岁的巨头？

主持人： What advantages do you guys have as a two-year-old company selling into the defense apparatus that a 70-year-old company selling into the same customer might not have?

Uwe： In that field, that segment of the market — the inexpensive, the AI-driven, the mass scalable systems (our strike drones come to mind, but also for example unmanned boats, and things like that) — we have a startup DNA. We built the prototypes like you would prototype in a startup, pretty much. And we built them from the get-go to be mass manufacturing items, which is not something that defense typically does.

When we walk into our factories — we just a few days ago had some operational experts and they looked at us like, "Oh, this is about as complex as a washing machine." And I don't know if they tried to insult those, but it is exactly where I want to be. Like if I tell you, "Hey Pat, today we're building a thousand washing machines a month, we need to scale this to 10,000 a month or to a million a year," you would say, "Okay, I mean, it's not easy, but it's doable somehow." So that's where you want to be.

And the established primes are not necessarily great at that. They're really good at building those exquisite, very important, very expensive systems. And I think they still will play a big role. But there's a part of that industry where it's about rapid innovation, ongoing development, close to the customer, understanding the customer, and then building for mass scalability — where I think we have a pretty good edge.

六、Stark 的工程组织：像风投一样管理 program

主持人： Awesome. Johannes, can you say a word about the product engineering organization and, as Uwe was saying, how do you execute on kind of the rapid innovation close to the customer? It's not the thing we typically associate with hardware companies selling into defense. So say a bit about the organization and a bit about how you move fast.

Johannes： At its very core, Stark is an engineering company. It's everything we do. And so the way how we organized the company is by building programs that can act and build very autonomously. As Uwe said earlier, we're organizing the company almost and running it almost like a venture fund where we're building small startups in a startup.

Engineers who join Stark find themselves very quickly in a family — a program — that is very autonomous and works in a very cross-functional sense towards the mission of the program. That can be fully autonomous maritime systems, fully autonomous naval or aerial systems, strike drones, electronic warfare, or software.

主持人： And is there a platform layer underneath these different programs? How does that work?

Johannes： Exactly. The programs serve external customers, and then there is a platform layer that we call capability teams, and they build capabilities that augment the ecosystem that we're creating. For example: GNSS-denied navigation, object classification, target reidentification, communication links, how we go about flight control. There are certain pieces that we then bring back as compounding value into the family of systems, into the programs.

As an engineer, you always either want to work on a platform and help the entire family of systems, or you want to be rather customer-centric, focusing on a customer, and work on a frontline system.

最自豪的能力：亚米级精度

主持人： Which capabilities are you most proud of today?

Johannes： We're extremely proud about being very very accurate at hitting targets. That's what we're extremely good at.

主持人： What does that take?

Johannes： It took us a very integrated approach to bringing hardware and software systems tightly integrated together. Just building a hardware system is good, but just building a separate isolated software stack that would be able to cope in a simulation, for example, is not enough.

The actual sub-meter precision for striking a tank or a moving target that moves at a speed of 60 km/h requires to fine-tune and get the settings in the parameterization — in terms of compute, compute budget, and memory allocation — all perfectly well done for the system to fulfill its purpose. And that is what we're very very proud of, that we accomplished.

七、"淬火"时刻：四周内扭转一次失败测试

主持人： You guys had a moment a year ago-ish where there's an experiment you were running and the experiment didn't quite hit the mark. And it's an experiment, so experiments don't always hit the mark, but it was reported that there's a big hubbub about how it failed. And you had four weeks or something to turn it around and conduct an even harder test. Can you just say a word about how it felt to go through that? How did the team rally to get the job done? And maybe the details on what was it you were trying to do.

Johannes： That was a forging moment for Stark. Stark in many regards was born out of fire, but that was a particular moment.

Just to get the context right: we had a major upgrade in one of our systems — the Virtuous system — that was hardware as well as software. As always, every engineer knows that you have a regression. If you have an update, then the center of gravity is off, or since the opening angle of the camera changed, you have to retrain some of your edge perception model. That's just how it is.

However, the Bundeswehr — the German bund army — asked us to participate in a very important experiment. And so we couldn't say no to that. And so we went there with a system that we knew is not at our ambition level, but at the same time we also couldn't decline, because we also thought that the step wasn't so big. And so we weren't able to fully test. That's number one. Number two is also that we tested that in an environment that was not ideal for the setup that we were at at this time.

However, the media was all about it. They knew that they wanted to bring us towards the edge and stress us out. And so that was, in their mind, actually not that bad. However, media caught this up and went all about it.

All hands on deck：三班倒 + 温泉酒店 + DIY 器材

Johannes： What we did is essentially an all-hands-on-deck meeting. We said, "Okay, everybody, this is a make-or-break moment for the company. This is where true engineering excellence will show. So the best minds of the engineering community at Stark have to come together."

We booked a three-star spa hotel — for the purpose of just being close to the shooting range where we had access to at the time. It was in November actually. It was extremely cold. And we worked three shifts around the clock.

While the flight test team went out, collected data, they were sending that back. We had at that time several containers set up. We had even mobile generators installing. We had, basically bought from DIY stores, very very quickly set up base in order to have the necessary infrastructure to collect data. And so as the flight test team was flying, it was extremely cold. The software engineers took that data and continued to work optimizing the full stack — flight test as well as perception. At the same time, parts of the hardware engineers also helped improve the actuation and tuned the system out.

In the course of actually only two weeks, we were getting to a hit accuracy that was perfect. There was this moment because we wouldn't — we said that we will only leave this place if we had three consecutive spot-on strikes. By then the tanks that we shot at were totally perforated. We wasted a lot of systems on that and they're not exactly cheap, right? But that was clear — no questions asked, money doesn't matter. We have to get to the precision.

We worked all 20-hour shifts. When the flight test team came back, the hardware engineers came back, repaired some of the systems. Since we were flying and shooting so much, we had to basically scrap some of the debris that we had from our own systems, put it back together in order to have a few more shots and stuff like that.

At the same time, the simulation team helped us further improve the flight dynamic modeling. We were employing AI systems at this time already to train flight dynamics modeling in order to improve the accuracy of the simulation so that our AI models can be trained within a simulation better. All these two workstreams then came together in the end. After two weeks — as a matter of fact, it was less than four weeks — there was this one moment where we realized, "okay, that's it." And from there on, we've always hit. We've always hit.

八、人才：到处去挖

主持人： Johannes, if you're building a software company today, it's very clear where the talent pools are. If you're building a defense company, it's not as clear. Tell us a little bit about how you find the best people and where you look.

Johannes： We look for talent in the classical industry, but also at universities. We're looking at startups. We're also looking at governmental institutions. We look everywhere because the talent that has to come together has to come from everywhere. It's such a breadth of functions that we need that, if it's very senior or very junior, we have to bring all the greatest minds together. If it's an existing established prime that usually comes with knowledge that is very very valuable — but at the same time the startup mindset is extremely and equally important.

主持人： So they're coming from different domains and different cultures. How do you stitch all that together and get it to work cohesively, particularly as you guys scale so quickly?

Johannes： So the programs build products for the outside world and they're cross-functional. Within each function, there are function heads that bring cohesiveness and consistency across electronic engineering, mechanical engineering and the various functions. They build communities of practice within the cross-functional teams. That's how we share knowledge, best practices, but also tooling decisions, AI approaches, AI workflows, skills, very important MCPs across the company.

国防不再是禁忌行业

Uwe： There's definitely something of a cultural shift in the tech and startup community. A few years ago, it would have been unimaginable for people to go into defense. It was not something you would do. And that is really changing.

We observe all over Europe, in all the countries basically, people understand this is a generational challenge, this is a generational task, it's time to step up for it. And we see people who have no touch point with defense before saying, "You know, maybe this is something for me." And for them, people like us specifically can be a good first touch point — because we are as much a defense company as we are a high-growth tech company. So we understand both worlds. For people who for the first time really want to apply their technical skills or their general skills into defense because they think, "Yeah, this is what I want to contribute," [we are] a very good first home, because we understand both sides. You don't need to have worked at defense if you want to work at Stark.

九、从起飞到打击：一次任务的全流程

主持人： Could you walk us through, as a way to illustrate the technology itself, a single strike from launch to strike — what's happening? What are all the different systems? What are the inputs and outputs? Can you walk us through that?

Johannes： For sure. I'm just wondering where to start, because [laughter] if I was to start at the logistics level — that's what matters. You don't win wars just because you strike, but it leads everything to the strike.

Working backwards from that, it always starts with the logistics. We just heard about the wooden boxes that are important. How do you disassemble and reassemble a system is extremely important. Then how do you transport it? Can it withstand the shocks and vibrations, the pressure, if it's transported by air or over sea? So there's various different environmental conditions that a system has to withstand. In some cases it actually had a shelf life of say 10 years until it actually gets deployed to the front line, where the system is then assembled or put on a catapult.

The concept of operations for all our systems is that an operator prepares the intent. So the system always implements and follows the intent. Think of it as a mission. The intent is modeled as no-fly zones or a kill zone or certain elements that comprise the mission. When the system then takes off, it automatically and autonomously finds its way, evading no-fly zones, evading anti-air installations, and flies its way. If it's in the combination with a swarm, communicating across the swarm what they see, so they share situational awareness across the members.

主持人： Would that work only if the swarm is all Stark products, or can it work — is there some communication that works across different [systems]?

Johannes： We're very open to that. We're extremely open, and we're going to speak probably about modularity as well. But just to finish that off: the system arrives at the kill zone, starts looking for the system, and then depending on how the customers implement human-in-the-loop, either the system fully autonomously seeks and destroys the target, or if there's a human-in-the-loop element, waits for a confirmation by the operator — and ultimately fulfills its mission.

主持人： It sounds like there's a lot of high-speed, very precise computer vision that is processing on the device.

Johannes： Correct. The units need to be fully autonomous. That requires perception. This perception is fed into a reasoning engine, to act upon the environment, the perception and the conditions in order to fulfill emissions. There's a higher order corridor, you may say.

主持人： Do you need to use your own ASIC to make that work?

Johannes： We do buy various different components from suppliers in order to make that work. There is an element of recency, as we always learn — there are new target types. The war in Ukraine is changing daily. So there is a lot of modularity and flexibility built into the systems. We're buying a lot of components that are procurable in large quantities, such as infrared cameras, electro-optical cameras, bring them together, sensor-fuse them in order to get a situational awareness onto the system in order to act autonomously.

十、垂直整合 vs. 生态系统

主持人： How do you guys think about where you need to be vertically integrated and where you want to leverage the ecosystem or the supply chain that's already in place?

Uwe： The governing principle for us is: how do we solve the customer issue? And the scalability of output is a big customer issue. So that would be my first question towards vertical integration — a strong argument for vertical integration is: can we solve the scalability issue through that? That's one force kind of pulling on that.

There's another force which goes exactly the opposite way, which is: it's so helpful for us if we sell those systems to other countries, if they can plug in their own suppliers — because we want to root the production of those systems in the countries in which they're being procured. So that's kind of the ongoing balance. Number one principle: can we solve the scaling issue? Number two: how can we plug in different suppliers to make everything more resilient?

单一产品 vs. 多产品

主持人： You've talked a lot about your strike drone product. What's your philosophy around being a single product company but being the best in the world at that one product, versus being multi-product since day one?

Uwe： We look towards where are those capability gaps. Those are basically self-described by the military — "Hey, we have a capability gap here" — and we observe them quite closely while they're being analyzed and formulated. Then we look at them: can we be a good supplier? How do we have a right to offer a solution for this? And is there one in the market?

That's the first exercise we do when thinking about the product portfolio. That pretty quickly also gets you to multi-product, because we don't see an abundance of offerings in the things that we do. So it's almost like a mandate — we have to try. We of course always have to counterbalance against the complexity and loss of focus of multiple programs. But I think our first initial reaction would be: there is a capability gap, it is evolving, we try to contribute to the definition of that gap, and then we probably will always ask ourselves: can we help, can we contribute?

Because multiple things on the technological side, on the understanding of the concept of operation side, can be taken, for example, from the aerial domain to the maritime domain. There is intent planning, mission planning — that doesn't matter if the asset is flying or swimming. There is navigation in denied environments where there's jamming — both happens in the maritime domain and in the aerial domain. There is object detection, recognition — again, the same. There's even some targeting — I'm homing in on a target. So there's a lot of things that we can use across domains, as we call them, or dimensions.

十一、制造：从 0 到真正规模

主持人： Can we talk about a topic that may sound boring on the surface, but it's really make-it-or-break-it for a company like you, which is manufacturing? How do you go from zero to manufacturing at real scale?

Johannes： There are two goals when we start a program. We optimize for time to market, and second, we optimize for production readiness. And they are often partially competing. If you're optimizing only for time to market, then you may end up relatively quickly with a product that you can show and demonstrate, but then it's very difficult to manufacture. For example, a Formula 1 car — you only build one. You're very quick to be ready, but you hardly ever produce them in large quantities.

From an engineering perspective, this has to happen: we shift left on manufacturability. That's extremely important, because otherwise you accrue a debt that you have to fix later on. That is really just the beginning, because the moment you decide on which components you buy, supply chain resilience plays a massive role in the decision-making process early on as well. We may not always buy — to the analogy of the washing machine — the greatest and most leading-edge camera. We buy those that are very very good, top quartile, but actually procurable in large numbers.

欧洲本地供应链现实吗？

主持人： People in defense talk a lot about local supply chains. Is that realistic in Europe, or do you have to look at say China or other countries as well?

Uwe： I think it is realistic. It is realistic specifically for certain components where it is fairly simple, and that's kind of the first step. "Oh yeah, here we can diversify and we can source from different suppliers and even from different countries." Conventional wisdom would be: well, is that good from a bottom-line profitability perspective? But it's probably good from a resilience perspective, and even more so, if your whole business is resilient.

There are still certain components where we have dependencies as the Western world entirely on, for example, Chinese supply, and so on so forth. We try of course to work on that and we reduce it dramatically. The current systems have hardly any reliance anymore. But there are also things where I think we as an industry, all of us, have to come together, with politics or militaries, and figure out what are the strategies on those things where raw chemicals, ingredients are needed, that go beyond the scope of just one company. It's probably more of an industrial coordination effort that's needed.

十二、AI 的位置：从任务规划到"失控"风险

主持人： Speaking of supply chain, I want to ask you about a very different part of your supply chain, which is AI. Part of the future of warfare is not just this move from exquisite systems to attractable systems — it's also the move from humans doing everything to more autonomous systems. We're kind of sitting here in the wake of the Hugging Face hack where these civilizations of agents, so to speak, broke out of their sandbox and wreaked havoc. So I guess I'm curious, given the power of the system and the inherent dangers in the product that you guys have, how do you think about the possibility of AI going rogue or somehow not working exactly the way that it's supposed to?

Johannes： Stark has since the beginning implemented NATO's principle of responsible use of AI. That entails that we're auditing our own systems not only by humans but also by safeguard layers that safeguard the AI in a corridor to be restricted to implement the operator's intent. That is what governs the entire autonomy stack at Stark, at every system and also at every stage of the mission.

Those are hard-coded constraints that, depending on where the system is — for example, if it's flying over a particular inhabited area, it may not arm — as one example. There are certain safeguards, and IEC 61508 and several things we borrowed from autonomous driving that we have learned, and that also found its way into our autonomous systems.

AI 到底出现在哪里？

主持人： More generally, I know that autonomy is kind of interwoven throughout the product and the operations of the product. Can you kind of sketch out — when we talk about autonomous systems, what does it mean? Where does the AI actually show up in the product or in the operations of the product?

Johannes： It shows up in every bit of the product, also in every part of the mission. Whenever there is a decision to be made — be it on what the system perceives, how the system interacts with its environment, also how the mission is planned on the ground before the system actually takes off. That's a very important aspect because mission planning used to be in the past very cumbersome and long.

主持人： Can we talk about that? How does AI play into mission planning? What's a good example?

Johannes： Imagine that there is a target coming in — very hands-on example — and that the operator has three systems at his or her disposal. Then the first decision to be made is: how many systems do I shoot at this target? What's the most cost-effective way of addressing this threat? That's the first decision to be made. Once that trade-off has been made, in our case the ground control system called Manurva optimizes the mission planning in order to address this threat accurately and most cost-effectively.

十三、既有巨头的问题 & 资本对比

主持人： You saw a gap in the markets and you went for strike drones, maritime drones and other products. Why haven't existing primes, traditional primes figured this out as well?

Uwe： I think they do to a certain degree. Sometimes more, sometimes less. Some of them have leaned into this, and sometimes some of them, including some that speak to us, say, "That's just not our DNA. We're not an organization that builds cheap systems. We are a company that is focusing on a different end of the market." And some are trying to —

We welcome that. I think one of the core ideas of what we need to do now is to start a competitive process. We want to compete against those people and their systems, and jointly we'll get better. At the end of the day, we're all on the same team. So some are trying, some are not so much, but we welcome all kinds of competition.

主持人： Arguably they have more capital than [you]. How do you think about that?

Uwe： Yes and no. If you look at — and that's maybe an interesting fact — if you just look at how much capital we intend to invest over the next 12, 24, 36 months, that's a sum of probably something like 600 million euros — significantly more than half a billion dollars, potentially much more. That's all going to go into research and development and product, production capability build-up.

When you just compare that to the orders of magnitude of spending — R&D spending of the big European primes — and if you subtract all the R&D spending that is government funded, but the actual core R&D spending that those companies do, we're not way off. That's not automatically a good thing. We want to stay nimble. We want to focus on our segment of the market. But we want to do meaningful contribution.

What I said earlier about understanding the customer, building exactly what the customer wants, getting that feedback from the staff sergeant — it needs to be different. Training, iterating with them. That's what we intend to do. And I think we're in a good position with the startup spirit, and now with the capital in our hands, to hopefully build a real pillar of the Western defense architecture.

十四、两年从 0 到 700 人：如何不乱？

主持人： You mentioned the capital you raised. You have done a lot in two years. You also went from zero to 700 people in two years. Is it chaos? How do you handle all of it? [laughter]

Johannes： So, first and foremost, the blueprints of the company need to be crystal clear. We spoke about that earlier. Number two: yes, growth always comes at the trade-off that there are sometimes hard decisions to be made. However, that is a process that is very manageable. We are improving towards our talent growth as always.

Generally, we feel that the blueprint works very well. But we also need to be clear that the problem that we're helping to solve is now. And so we have to be fast. We have to make a dent now. Being slow is not an option. Allocating these 700 — not all engineers, but the majority are engineers — to extremely important and valuable programs is key. This is what we set out to do. Are we at the end of the journey? Of course not. However, we're very determined to succeed in these programs.

十五、下一个难题：合同即威慑

主持人： Is there a very hard problem you're trying to solve right now? Is there something on the roadmap that you haven't figured out yet?

Johannes： What we always see in Ukraine is that systems are flying faster. That's something we are leapfrogging, going into as well a lot. We see that compute becomes more accessible. We're thinking a lot around how we can further drive AI on the systems in a safe manner, but give it more capabilities — for example, adjustable to targets that are on the naval side as well as maybe in the air, and not only on the ground. There are various areas we're going into, but also in the electromagnetic space, there is a massive disruption happening thanks to software-defined radios and affordable compute that allows to bring down costs for sensors of the electromagnetic space. That's extremely interesting.

Uwe： I'm really interested in solving the next big thing, which for me is kind of like the contractual design. Because I think there's a big deterrence possibility in the way we structure those contracts. It's one thing that we sell hundreds of thousands — or potentially tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands — of those systems. But what's really interesting is: can we come to a contractual design between the government and us, and potentially others actually, that already has everything in place for the massive surge in scaling that we need if there's ever hot conflict?

Because that would — very interesting. All of a sudden we maybe think about this more in terms of like cloud contracts, with surges and so on. Because we get that done. That is probably where the real deterrence comes from. It's not about the individual capabilities of one product here or there.

主持人： What would that look like? So there's some stockpile presumably, but then they prepave for manufacturing capacity that you can just spin up in the event of something?

Uwe： I mean, there's a big question about the supply chain. There's a big question about storage of systems. There's a big question about who updates those systems. If you look at a drone at the moment, probably the motors, they're good for three years, but software probably should be updated every week with new training data and so on. So how do we structure all of that? That's something that's very interesting to me. Because that's one way how you can create real deterrence, I think.

主持人： Has anyone in the Western world figured this out?

Uwe： I don't think so, necessarily. And there's not a blueprint. The same goes for all things that we do in procurement and all things we do in product development. There's not like hundreds of people who have done this and now they can just teach us. I think we all learn together. And by the way, that kind of crosses both sides — on the government side, on the military side, on the industrial side.

I do think there is an optimistic spirit of: okay, we need to figure out a few things, because we don't have the right toolset just yet. But in that spirit, we need to solve it together. I don't think somebody has the perfect playbook — "here's how it's done, just copy this." We don't have that yet. But it makes the whole thing so exciting. It's at the forefront of what's technologically possible. It is very clearly what's required to be able to survive in those battles. And bringing those two things together is kind of allowing us to make a real contribution to continue to live in peace.

十六、使命与五到十年后的世界

主持人： What is the mission of the company?

Uwe： The mission is quite clearly: we want to be one of the absolute pillars of our European and Western defense architecture. That means yes, we want to be a sizable company that specifically delivers the capabilities that we talked about, but we also want to help orchestrate a real innovation ecosystem. We want to be a good collaborator with other people. We want to work with the large ones, the small ones, our peers, with everybody.

Because when you think about it — the one mission for the company is very closely linked to all of our mission. That's very important for me to stress. We want to be a pillar of — of course a dominating pillar — but it's not a mission that can be achieved by one single company alone.

主持人： And if you do achieve the mission, and we're sitting here five or ten years from now, what does Stark look like? What does Europe look like? What does the world look like?

Uwe： I think Europe will become a better partner for the US again. There will be hopefully a new chapter of transatlantic cooperation. Europe is a helpful, strong, principled ally — among each other and towards the US and other partners in the world. And we live hopefully in more peaceful times, where we go back to how the world was a few years ago, and hopefully we have de-escalated some of the wars and situations around the world, and others have never flared up.

主持人： Amazing. Uwe, Johannes, thank you for joining us.

Uwe & Johannes： Thank you so much. Thank you.
