item.title: [a16z] Amazon CEO Andy Jassy on the $220 Billion AI Buildout
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

1. 这不是三次独立战略，是同一个剧本演了三遍

Jassy 这场访谈里最被忽略的事实是：他正在用同一套剧本跑第三轮，而几乎没有人识别出这个模式。

  • 2001–2003：内部基础设施痛点 → 诞生 AWS
  • 2022：履约网络过度建设 → 区域化重构 → 速度与成本双降
  • 2024–2026：AI 算力稀缺 → 垂直整合 + 2200 亿美元 CapEx

而最微妙的证据藏在 Annapurna 这桩收购里。Jassy 亲口承认：他们当年不是为了 AI 芯片而买的 Annapurna，最初只是想做一张虚拟化网卡（NIC），把服务器"几乎 100% 让给计算"。但同一个团队后来做出了 Graviton，又做出了 Tranium。换句话说，Annapurna 是一个被买下的"芯片期权"——Jassy 当年并不知道未来需要什么芯片，但他知道自己需要一个可被反复召唤的芯片团队。十年后这个期权兑现为对抗 Nvidia 的筹码。这是教科书级别的"可选性资产（optionality asset）"投资，但以收购形态呈现，让大多数观察者看不懂它的真正估值逻辑。

2. 哑铃的"中空"才是 2200 亿美元的真正目标

Jassy 把 AI 需求描绘成哑铃——一端是支付任何价格的 AI 实验室，另一端是追求降本的企业。然后他说出了那句关键话：哑铃的中间是空的，而且这个"中空"才是未来最大的绝对市场。

更出人意料的是他紧接着承认——推理成本"仍然贵了一个数量级"。

把这两点连起来，一个反直觉的结论浮现：2200 亿美元的 CapEx 根本不是为了服务今天 AI 实验室的需求。那只是过渡现金流。Amazon 真正的赌注是——用极致规模把推理价格压下一个数量级，撬开一个今天还不存在的市场。

这是"Build it and they will come"的反转版：Build it so that the price point at which they can come actually exists. 不是服务既有需求，而是人为制造价格断崖，让一个被成本封印的市场破壁爆发。所以这场 CapEx 军备竞赛，表面上在抢实验室订单，底层却是一个关于"推理成本曲线斜率"的赌博。

3. 跨领域连接：数据中心是这个时代的"核电站"

Jassy 甩出一个锐利的数据——高尔夫球场消耗的水是所有数据中心的 200 倍，杏仁产业更不用提。但只有数据中心被政治化、妖魔化。

为什么？这里藏着一个被忽略的视觉认知机制：

  • 高尔夫球场从空中看是绿色的、像森林——视觉上被归类为"自然"
  • 数据中心是灰色方盒子——视觉上被归类为"工业"

人类的投票并不基于数据，而基于视觉类别。这与煤电 vs. 核电的政治经济学完全同构——煤电死亡率远超核电，但煤的危害是不可见的 PM2.5，核的危害是可想象的蘑菇云。于是我们禁核电、补贴煤电。

数据中心正在成为 2020 年代的核电站：一个可见的替罪羊，承载着对分布式、不可见问题（电网几十年投资不足）的愤怒。而真正讽刺的是——如果 Jassy 是对的，这些数据中心最终反而会把当地电价压下去（他举了 Indiana、Georgia、Mississippi 的例子）。被妖魔化的东西，恰恰是解决被归咎问题的那把钥匙。

4. 最被低估的洞察：我们正在逆转工业革命

Bedrock 团队那个数字——6 名工程师，76 天，替代"40 人一年"——是约 10 倍的生产力跳跃。听起来像福特 1908 年的流水线革命（也是约 10 倍）。

但方向上存在一个关键反转：

  • 福特流水线降低了每个工人的技能要求（装一个螺栓就够了）
  • AI 协作提升了每个工人的技能跨度（一人要跨前端、后端、设计、产品）

我们不是在从"手工艺"走向"工厂"，而是在从"工厂"倒退回"手工艺"——但保持了工厂级别的产出。

Jassy 自己说中了这一点："公司变大后，产品经理只负责一个切片——定价、或某个功能。"过去 25 年的组织专业化正在被 AI 快速解绑。文艺复兴式的"全才"回归了，只不过现在每个全才背后站着一群 agent。

这不是单纯的生产力革命，这是组织形态的时代倒流。Jassy 预言的"更少的人、更小的团队、重写一切"，本质上是说：公司将变得更像中世纪手工作坊，而不是更像现代工厂。

5. 一个藏在"安全"段落里的黑色幽默

Jassy 几乎顺口提到一个巨大断言：公司未来必须在"几分钟内"部署安全补丁——而且几乎所有应用都必须被重写成"可被 agent 更新"的形态。

把这句话拆开看：

  • 过去 30 年软件工程追求的核心价值之一是——代码的稳定性、不可随意变更、变更要经过人类审查
  • Jassy 现在说：对不起，所有这些都要翻转。你必须让 agent 可以在几分钟内改你的生产代码。

这意味着——软件工程的根基价值观正在被 180 度翻转，但大多数企业甚至还没意识到这场范式转移已经发生。那些以"治理严格"为傲的大型组织，可能恰恰是最脆弱的。因为他们的治理体系本身就是为"人类改代码"设计的，不是为"agent 改代码"设计的。安全从"围墙高度"问题，正在变成"反应速度"问题——而这是一个完全不同的游戏。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open: $220 Billion and Still Not Enough

Even spending $220 billion this year, we're leaving a meaningful amount of demand on the table. We always leave a certain amount for on-demand, but '26 is obviously sold out. '27 is largely sold out. A good chunk of '28 is sold out.

The financial markets are saying, "Oh, there's not enough money in the world to finance these things." Everything we do in the world today — stock market, banking, healthcare — they're all using data centers. Our job is to try to figure out how to have as much capacity as we can. We have an opportunity to help across so many more customer experiences and make their lives better and easier every day.

The big labs being willing to pay almost anything for power, cooling, chips — well, maybe we should buy out the old guys and sell them to the new guys because they'll pay us whatever.

Andy, welcome to the podcast. It's great to have you.

Thanks for having me.

2021 → 2026: How Amazon Has Changed

So you're five years into running Amazon, and you've done a lot since being here, and a lot is coming out as CEO. Right now, $220 billion in CapEx spend, AWS growing 28%. How do you think about the ambition in 2026 relative to 2021 when you took over formally as CEO?

Oh, 2021 feels so long ago — it feels like a decade ago. But the world changes fast, and if you compare it to 2021, our overall top line is about 80% higher, our AWS business about almost three times bigger, our ads revenue about two and a half times bigger. So the business has just grown quite a bit.

I think there are a few things that have really happened. Pretty quickly after I started in the role — which was on the tail end of the pandemic — in our retail business, we ended up with a real cost-to-serve challenge where we had basically doubled the size of our fulfillment network that we'd built over 25 years. We doubled the size of it in about 18 months. And then we built the last-mile transportation network the size of UPS in about 20 months.

Whenever you build that quickly, you end up with all sorts of things that you don't have optimized. Our cost to serve in our fulfillment network were not what we wanted, and it created a lot of challenges and angst. A lot of people at that time — I remember, it was just a year or so, a little less than a year into starting the job — people said, "Boy, what a terrible time to start, what bad luck."

In retrospect, it was really a great time to start and a real blessing, because it allowed us to consider a bunch of things that we probably wouldn't have considered for many years, but they were really good ideas for our customers and for the business. The biggest of which in our fulfillment network ended up being that we regionalized a flat national fulfillment network in the US. We regionalized it so we got items much closer to customers, which both lowered our cost to serve — because of shorter transportation distances — while getting items to customers much more quickly. That reevaluation of our most closely held beliefs during that time when we were struggling on cost to serve really unleashed speed of delivery and a lot of demand in our retail business, and was a big piece of why we've grown as fast as we have there.

The AI Explosion

Of course, pretty quickly thereafter, AI exploded further on the scene. It's not like AI was new — we've been doing machine learning for a long time, and there have been lots of waves of AI that were supposed to be the real tipping points. But you get to 2023 and you really see with generative AI a huge difference.

Our AWS business was growing really quickly at that point. We have the broadest functionality by a fair bit, stronger operational performance and security, and I think a type of partner ecosystem that is different. We were the clear leader and we felt like that business could be a few hundred billion dollars of revenue over a long period of time — figure over 10 years.

Now we look at what's happening with AI and how every customer experience we know of is going to be reinvented with inference and AI. We actually think the AWS business — not only is it growing really rapidly, I mean last quarter we grew 36.7% year-over-year on a $169 billion annual revenue run-rate business — the opportunities today are really striking.

If you layer on top of that the seeds that we have of new businesses: how the team has progressed our Prime Video business (which is now a large and profitable business), or the low-Earth-orbit satellite we're building with Amazon Leo, or the autonomous driving / ride-hailing service with Zoox, or our healthcare business, or what we're doing in robotics — we have an opportunity to help so many more customers across so many more customer experiences and make their lives better and easier every day. That mission of trying to make customers' lives better and easier every day really unifies everything we're doing across the company.

Building Fast Without Lowering the Bar

You mentioned that when you're building out the fulfillment network so fast, it's going to be a little inefficient. From a CEO perspective, how do you communicate what you're doing without lowering the cultural standard of operating efficiency and frugality?

What's interesting is we have this set of leadership principles that a lot of people know about — we have 16 leadership principles. They govern the way we think about operating as a team and culturally. But there are several that are in tension with one another. Sometimes people are confused about that, but the reality is it just reflects the way the real world works. Nothing is really perfectly clean. You're always making trade-offs.

If you go back to that time when we made the decision to build out the fulfillment network and the last-mile transportation network that aggressively, that quickly, the question the team was facing was: we know if we go this fast, it's going to be really hard. It'll probably be more expensive than if we went slower. We will probably not get everything as optimally as we would if we went slower. But customers and sellers really need it. So are we going to actually shade on the side of enabling? Remember back then, in the early part of the pandemic, no physical stores were open. If you look at the role Amazon played in everybody's lives during the pandemic, it was very seminal.

So we had to ask ourselves: are we going to build fast — and maybe not as optimally as we can — with the trade-off of serving customers and sellers who are trying to also have businesses that sustain themselves? Or not? That's the first decision you have to make. And we decided, as we almost always do, to shade on the side of customers.

Then it was fairly obvious that as we were building, not everything we were planning was going perfectly. Our fulfillment team was more in the office than most of the rest of the company, but still a lot of people had to participate in a lot of the designing and planning and assessing. Now you're balancing the combination — or the tension — of bias for action/speed, and relentlessly high standards, which means you deliver at the cost structure and the delivery and the design that you'd always planned for. You have to make trade-offs. We made the trade-off to side with customers and to move quickly to be able to serve sellers and consumers, and we thought there'd be some amount of cleanup.

Now, did we know exactly how the topography would work out the way it did? No. And there were certain things that we didn't have optimized that I'm not sure we foresaw wouldn't be optimized. But if you have good metrics, and if you're a culture that's a truth-telling culture — which is another really important part of our culture — we get the data on the table, we get the issues on the table, we're direct with one another, we don't allow people to paper over issues. If you have that type of culture, it's fairly obvious in the metrics and in the discussion. Then you just have to go about figuring out how you want to improve it, and which pieces are just small productivity things and which are architectural pieces. We went back and really re-architected key parts of the network after we got that capacity installed — something that at the time for that team was maybe eight or nine on their list of priorities, but became a much higher priority as a way to actually get the combination of speed and cost.

"Build It and They Will Come" — At $220 Billion Scale

Fascinating. At the beginning, when you started AWS, it was kind of "build it and they will come." But this is that at a much bigger scale. You and others are building data center and chip capacity so fast that the financial markets are saying things like, "There's not enough money in the world to finance these things." How do you know how much is too much?

It's a very good question. And I wish there was an equation that would make it simple — it would save us a lot of time as a team.

In the first wave of cloud, when we started AWS, we didn't know if people would use it. So "build it and they will come." But we had very good signals inside the company — this was around the early part of the 2000s. We had teams that were not moving nearly as quickly as we wanted them to, even though we felt like relatively we moved quickly. We just couldn't understand why it took so long. It turned out that our product teams were spending 70 to 80% of their time on the infrastructure pieces, which didn't differentiate them, and only about 20% of their time on what differentiated the product pieces. Every team was doing it and reinventing the wheel.

So we originally conceived of AWS to allow ourselves to move more quickly internally. We figured if we built a set of high-scale, high-availability, low-cost, highly flexible building block services — compute, storage, database, content distribution, messaging — we would be able to build much quicker in our consumer business. Then we said: we're pretty good, relatively speaking, technically; probably other companies have the same issues. Even before we launched externally, we had so many teams internally interested that we knew we were on the right track. I don't think any of us anticipated it would grow as fast as it did externally.

The 100x–400x Difference With AI

On the AI side, there have been these different waves of people saying, "This is the time, AI is finally here." Even six, seven years before the generative AI wave, people felt like it was AI's time, and we built a whole bunch of AI services — that actually was a pretty good business for us on the AWS side, but nothing like what we're seeing right now.

In the early days of AWS, we felt like we were growing really fast and we felt good about it. We were about a $60 million annual run-rate business after three years. In the first three years of this generative AI wave, just our AI business in AWS is over $25 billion in run rate. It's several hundred times faster. We just haven't seen anything like it.

Then the question becomes: how much CapEx do you want to invest to go after the opportunity? We've said this year — in 2026 — we expect to spend about $220 billion of CapEx. I remember being at leadership team breakfast 15 years ago when we couldn't believe the telco companies spent $50 billion in CapEx — we were like, "They're really spending that much on CapEx?" So these numbers are kind of mind-blowing. And even spending $220 billion in CapEx this year, we're leaving a meaningful amount of demand on the table.

Two Macro Buckets of CapEx

The thing that helps us here is that we have really good visibility into customer demand. If you think about the CapEx investments in AWS and the way the cash cycle works, there are two macro areas: investment for data centers, and investment for servers and networking.

  • Data centers — you have to invest about two years in advance of when you can put servers in and start to monetize. The good news is you only make that investment once; it's a useful-life asset of about 30 years, but you make it a couple of years in advance.
  • Server and networking gear — depending on the component, it's only a few months in advance. You have very good visibility into customer demand before you pull that trigger. If it turns out you don't actually need the capacity to fill those data centers, you won't buy the server/networking gear. On average, they tend to break even in about three years, and have useful lives at this point of about five to six years. And most of the deals we're doing are about five-year deals.

When you are building as fast as we're building with so many data centers simultaneously, you're going to spend a lot of capital and your free cash flow is going to have headwinds in those years — until you get to those later stages, a few years down the road, where all those data centers are in-line and being monetized and you're making back your money from the server and network investment. Because of the way the cash cycle works, it has headwinds in the early years when you're growing that fast.

Data Centers Become Political

Data centers going back when you started AWS were probably the last thing in the world you would believe would be a political issue. But here we are — particularly in the US, nobody anywhere in the world is as anti-data-center as US politics. Is there any merit to the anti-data-center argument?

Well, I'll give you some context that I have, or at least I believe. If you think about everything we do in the world today — stock market, banking, healthcare, entertainment, shopping, education, business, ride-hailing — everything we do is digitally driven. They're all using data centers in a very similar way. Nobody is saying, "I'm anti-me — I don't want to use my phone anymore." They all use data centers.

That's before AI. AI is the biggest technology transformation of our time, which I think is saying something, since we've lived through the internet, the cloud, and mobile. The reality is the type of infrastructure buildout we need to support the rapid growth we were just talking about on the AI side — there hasn't been anything like it in the world, and in this country since maybe when we built out the highways and bridges in the 1950s. That's the type of buildout we're going through. And the country — I think the world in general, but I'd say the US specifically — cannot afford not to build data centers, or we will find that another country like China will establish all the leadership and all the norms there. I don't think any of us are going to like that, either domestically or globally. So we have to build data centers.

Myths vs. Realities

Now, do I think there are ways we can be doing it better, all of us as an industry? Of course. It's happening quickly and everybody's learning together. But there are a number of what I would consider somewhere between myths and mistruths right now being propagated, because it's one of those issues where you have an easy villain — and politically, opportunists like to find that villain to point at.

  • Water: The golf industry or the almond farming industry consume way more water than data centers do. Our data centers — golf courses consume 200 times more water than all our data centers. They consume more in two days than we do in a year in our data centers.
  • Pollution / generators: When you register new sites and you have backup generators, you have to register and show the amount if you ran all of those generators full-time at full capacity. But of course it never happens. You only run backup generators 0.1 of 1% of the year — like 10 hours a year for maintenance.
  • Energy rates: If you look in the different geographies in which we have a big data center presence, some rates have gone up, some have gone down. But the real issue is that as a country we have not invested in the infrastructure of our grids the way we've needed to. There's going to be meaningful growth, and something was going to push it over to investment. It just turns out that AI, because it's growing so rapidly and significantly, is the thing that pushed it over. Once you actually get that capacity, in most of the geographies, the rates will flatline or go down — as they have in Indiana, Georgia, Mississippi.
  • Taxes & community investment: In these geographies, the big data center providers are paying a lot of tax. If you look in St. Joseph County in Indiana, we've paid about $3 billion of tax. The communities get that money and get to spend it on things that really matter. We've built programs like Built Together — we just committed another billion dollars in the communities in which we have data center presence over the next five years.

We have to keep working on it with the communities — it has to be a public and private partnership. But the buildout is so important to the future of the country. Imagine if we hadn't built out highways and bridges, what the economic prosperity and capabilities of the country would be. We have to keep it in perspective, and we have to be partners in the communities in which we build.

The Barbell of AI Demand

Let's go back to the CapEx for a second. The $220 billion — that's $600 million a day. How do you think about AI demand right now? Offline we were talking about how you see it as a barbell.

The first context piece is what I said earlier: I can't believe how big and fast AI has grown. It's a few hundred times faster than the beginning of AWS in the first three years — $25 billion run rate for us just in AI revenue in AWS in the first three years. So it's really large.

And yet it really is barbelled if you look at how demand is:

  • One end of the barbell: the AI labs, who are consuming gobs and gobs of compute unlike anything I've seen. And then a few runaway apps — ChatGPT, Claude Code, things like that.
  • Other end of the barbell: enterprises who are largely using AI for cost avoidance and productivity — automating customer service, fraud, business process automation.
  • The middle of the barbell: the current production workloads of enterprises, many of which are using AWS and using inference today — but the overwhelming majority of which still aren't in any pervasive way.

That middle, I think, is going to be the largest absolute segment of AI usage. It's hard for me to predict the rate at which it will happen. It's happening to a greater extent every year. But if you zoom out five to seven years, I think quite a few — if not most — of the enterprise applications that we use and that exist today are going to be using inference in a pervasive way. There is a lot of growth in front of us.

Scarcity, Pricing, and Not Squeezing Core Customers

Faced with the big labs being willing to pay maybe anything for power, cooling, chips — and your long-time customers paying regular rates — is there business pressure to buy out the old guys and sell to the new guys?

It's a good question. We don't think of it quite the way you're talking about, but I can completely understand. If you think about it, there's only so much data center and power today. There's only so much memory, and I don't think that shortage ends in 2027.

One of the reasons I think we can invest a lot more and it wouldn't be a bad use of capital is: '26 is obviously at this point sold out. '27 is largely sold out — we always leave a certain amount for on-demand in our inference service Bedrock or EC2, but largely sold out all the big chunks. A good chunk of '28 is sold out. There's so much demand.

If you have the AI business and what we call the core business (think of "core" as non-AI), they're both growing at really rapid rates right now. If you have only a certain amount of memory, you have to decide how much to allocate to HBM — to the AI accelerators — versus to DRAM for your core. These are real trade-offs.

Customer-First Allocation

Where we start on this issue is being customer-focused. We have deep relationships and partnerships with our customers in AWS. The same as during the pandemic — unlike our competitors who tried to figure out how to optimize within quarters to drive revenue as much as possible in a world where companies were going to cost-optimize — we took a different approach. We proactively had our field go out and help customers figure out how they could cost-optimize, even though we knew it would diminish our revenue short- and medium-term. We're going to help our customers be successful, because our very strong belief is: if we help customers over a long period of time, our business will come along with it.

That's the same thing here on the core. You could do calculations and decide that because of the scarcity and their willingness to pay, you have customers who would pay more to squeeze out your core customers — but they're running their businesses on top of AWS. They're running all their core applications. We're not going to squeeze our customers. We're going to make sure they can scale. Then our job is to try to figure out how to have as much capacity as we can to allow not just our core customers, but all of our customers who want to use us on the AI side to be able to do so — and do so in a way where it's sustainable economically for us as well.

I wish I could tell you I thought the supply constraints would just be a 2027 issue. I think we'll see them in different components for several years. We're probably putting more capacity in than anybody else, because we continue to be very passionate about continuing to be the significant leader in the infrastructure and AI space, like we've been. We're spending $220 billion this year, and we could spend a lot more — it wouldn't be a bad use of capital, both medium-to-long-term — and I think we still probably wouldn't satisfy all the demand. There is just incredible demand right now.

The Annapurna Story: Buying a Team, Not a Chip

You did something back in 2015 when you bought Annapurna Labs — probably before you were thinking about giant AI demand. What drove that decision, and how is it paying off now?

The Annapurna team is one of the most talented teams and set of people I've ever had a chance to work with. It's one of the very best acquisitions we've done at Amazon in the history of the company — if not the best.

We foresaw some pieces, but we did not make the Annapurna purchase for AI chips per se. When you get to a certain scale, you start to have access and visibility to patterns of customers at very large scale that you realize: if you can vertically integrate and build certain capabilities yourself, you'll be able to provide more value for customers and better economics for the business.

Starting With the NIC

What Annapurna started as for us was: on the core EC2 server, we felt like we were using too much of the server for virtualization, networking, security, and storage. We wanted to be able to use nearly 100% of the server for compute for customers. We had been working with Annapurna before we acquired them on this NIC that offloaded those components to the NIC, to allow us to have as much of the server for compute as possible. We really liked the team, we really liked the product we collaborated on, and we realized this was going to end up being in virtually every EC2 server. It's turned out to be in every server we have.

From NIC to Graviton

We originally bought it because that was going to be a core capability of our compute capabilities. And because the team was so talented at building chips, we felt like they could probably build other chips too. At that time, we had a very deep partnership — which we still have — with Intel. But Intel had virtually all of the CPU share. When you have a partner who has virtually all the share, they're not often thinking about how to drive price-performance. They're trying to think about other features that allow them to get more share and drive more revenue. By the way, it's totally understandable — these are the dynamics of how markets work. It's part of how the innovator's dilemma comes up.

We tried to push on price-performance and it was hard for us to get attention. But we had customers who wanted to move more and more of their on-premises workloads to the cloud and they wanted better price-performance. So the next thing we turned the Annapurna team loose on was to build a CPU chip — and they built Graviton. 99% of our top thousand EC2 customers use it very pervasively today. It's about 40% more price-performance than other x86 processors. That has been hugely impactful for our customers and our business.

Then Tranium

A few years ago we saw that same movie in the AI space, where you really had one dominant provider who's very good — we had a deep partnership with them, we still have one, we will for as long as I can foresee. But they have giant markets and lots of different products they're building and priorities. We knew our customers needed better price-performance. That's why we spun out a separate team in Annapurna to build an AI accelerator, which we call Tranium — also about 30% to 40% more price-performance than other comparable processors.

Why Inference Cost Matters So Much

When you talk about that middle of the barbell, if you ask what are the things that will change that middle to have more current enterprise production apps using inference, there are a couple of things. Some of it is talent — being comfortable doing post-training and fine-tuning, having the organizational muscle that knows how to prioritize what to go after and how to do it. But a big, big chunk of it is the cost of inference.

The cost of inference has come down quite a bit in the last few years, but it's still an order of magnitude too expensive, in my opinion, for it to be used as pervasively as possible. If you're asking enterprises to rewrite their applications that use CPU today with AI accelerators, and the difference in those costs is very significant, the amount of incremental benefit they have to get from having the AI accelerators is a much higher bar to want to rewrite those apps. But if you take the cost of inference down, that bar is much lower, and all applications are going to be better and smarter and more capable with AI accelerators and inference. So driving the cost of inference down is a really important part of customers being able to use AI pervasively — and our chips business is a big piece of that.

I can tell you from our own firm that it can get very expensive. We had one employee spend $2 million in the last — doing good work — I was like, "Okay, this inference is not that cheap."

Yeah.

Investing in Anthropic and OpenAI

One of the things you've done is you've made some investments, particularly in Anthropic and OpenAI — I think $18 billion in Anthropic and $50 billion in OpenAI or something like that. What got you to want to do that? That and similar investments from Nvidia and so forth got Wall Street up in a tizzy because it reminded them of the bad old days of the dot-com boom. Why did it make sense, particularly since they are also customers?

Both of those companies are really impressive teams and really impressive companies. The rate at which they've grown their businesses, at least in the top line — I don't know if we've ever seen anything like it. It's really unbelievable.

To us it's a combination of:

  • Who these teams are
  • The technology and models they've built
  • Some of the applications they've built
  • Our belief in how transformative AI is
  • The fact that we believe these are going to be two of the most successful companies in the space over a long period of time

Not everyone's going to be a winner, but there are going to be a lot of very successful companies in this space, and we believe these will be two of them. And we partner so closely.

Anthropic

Starting with Anthropic, where we've had the longer partnership — we have so many customers that run Anthropic in Bedrock, our inference service. I think customers are most successful running Anthropic in Bedrock. We have had a deep partnership with them on chips, where they've been building on top of Tranium for a while. I think it's been very good for Anthropic, I think it's been very good for our Tranium team, I think we both learned quite a bit from each other. So we have a deep partnership with them where both our belief in the future of AI and the partnership made it make sense to make investments as part of those partnerships.

OpenAI

On the OpenAI side, we just had so many customers who wanted to use OpenAI and AWS and weren't able to do so because of their prior business arrangements. For a long time, I think the companies had a lot of mutual respect and desire to work together. Over a series of conversations and months — the ability to be able to run OpenAI in Bedrock, the fact that we built a unique product together in the stateful runtime environment (which is how I think all agents are going to be built moving forward; you're going to need state), like Anthropic, they made a multi-year, multi-gigawatt commitment to Tranium — and we just believe that is going to be one of the most successful companies in the space over a long period of time.

All those made it make sense for us to have deeper partnerships and investments.

Organizational Redesign in the AI Era

Switching over to how you use AI to build a company. I think you said the Bedrock team rebuilt your inference engine with six engineers in 76 days — and that would have taken 40 people a year. That's pretty different. Amazon is famous for the two-pizza teams. What's your current organizational design thinking?

I agree with what you're saying. The Bedrock experience you alluded to was very eye-opening for everybody here. We spent a bunch of time sharing that story internally to inspire people and remind people what's possible.

Over time, what ends up happening — I started the company 29 years ago. I started as an assistant product manager, and I was the product manager for, I don't know, five products. Today, when companies get successful and bigger and the products get bigger, a product manager works on one product and they just own one slice of it. They own pricing — or they do just one thing. Everybody becomes more specialized, and everybody accepts that that's the way you have to do business if you're building something big and successful. And it's not. It's definitely not when you look at what's happening with AI.

A Weekend-Scale Prototype

If I look at the last week, we're working on some things around agents in our consumer business — we have a whole bunch of investments there. We had an idea we really liked that we agreed on Thursday we were going to try, and we wanted to have a real working prototype. Four or five people, over the weekend, had it operating in an 80% shippable way by Sunday. That is a different world you live in.

What It Means for Future Organizations

  • Fewer humans doing the work. If you look at the amount of coding being done agentically, the amount of customer service and business intelligence and research — fast-forward to how spreadsheets are going to be built, the number of lawyers you have. You're not going to have no people, but you're not going to have as many humans as we've all thrown at scale as businesses have gotten bigger. In the future there are going to be different jobs and new jobs — some we know about, some we don't — that will arise as AI and robotics and space develop.
  • Smaller teams. People who can work cross-functionally — they don't only own one sliver, because the model is going to be able to get them 80% of the way there in a lot of these different functions. Every team will start at a much more advanced stage than we have in the past, and you'll be able to invent much more expansively and much more quickly.
  • Agentic-native vs. legacy. Startups starting today, most of them are starting agentically, AI-native right from the start. All the larger companies who've been in business for a while are going to have to figure out how to build at that same pace. Some of them will figure it out — and when you have a big business with a lot of capabilities and a loyal customer base, that's great. Some of them will move very slowly to figure it out and they will be more vulnerable, in my opinion, than startups.
  • Rewriting code to be agent-updatable. I predict that companies will have to rewrite almost all their code to be agentically capable. You're going to have to allow agents to be updating different pieces of code. You're going to have to build constraints there.

The Real Near-Term AI Risk: Cybersecurity

If you just look at security, it's kind of interesting. If you look at all of the nervousness of the last month or two about models, they are focused on the more fantastical scenarios. By the way, they're possible. Is it possible an evil botnet will take over everything? I guess it's possible. It's possible you can infuse robots with malicious intent. They're all possible, I personally think we're going to figure that out together as an industry and public-private segment. You've got to start by paying attention to some of these things.

But the thing that's interesting is that I don't think there is enough discussion about the more immediate-term risks, which are really around cybersecurity. These models find so many more vulnerabilities than you did before — than humans weren't finding (maybe you could argue if they could or couldn't, but they just weren't finding).

So if you fast-forward, I think the way applications are going to have to be able to respond to imminent security threats is going to be in minutes. Today, you find vulnerabilities, people classify them, people develop patches. Even if you do that part quick, most companies take a long time to deploy because there are all these dependencies. You're going to have to deploy in minutes. If you don't actually have your applications rewritten to be able to be updated by agents, you're going to have no chance in that new world.

I just think all organizations are going to be reinvented. The companies that prioritize this are going to be in much better shape than those that don't.

It seems like we as an industry did not do a great job of architecting everything — from the big systems to embedded devices — with good security architecture. The day of reckoning is here. The good news is that's a big opportunity for new companies, new efforts.

Almost every partner and customer we talk to on the AWS side — every company of any size — is worried about the security piece. We've got a professional services practice where we're helping a lot of customers, and we've built a service called Continuum that identifies a lot of these vulnerabilities and builds patches. But it's easier to said than done. A lot of companies and a lot of engineers — it isn't exciting sometimes to focus on the security piece. It's easy to wait until there are problems. If you protect data that matters, it's a bad idea.

Also, in most companies — going back to our earlier conversation — specialization has probably been the worst case in security, where you've got these very esoteric security engineers who don't like working with the other engineers, who are a scarce resource, and so on. As a result, in most companies' software, their security practices just aren't that good. The good news is we have tools that will help with that.

The good-news part of it is: you have to hire pen testers — there are only so many security people you're going to hire, and only so many applications they can get to. The models coupled with automation are going to allow you to better pen-test your entire surface, and you're going to find things that you might not have otherwise found outside of a fluke.

Three Approaches to AI, and the Alexa Reinvention

You can do a lot of things with AI. One: cut costs — reduce the number of accountants, lawyers. There are even VC firms saying, "We'll buy old companies and cut their costs." Two: build something the world's never seen. Three: what you've done with Alexa — rethink an existing successful product from the beginning because of this new platform. How do you decide when the third makes sense?

I think that's actually an interesting delineation. Organizations, as we just talked about, are going to really change and get more streamlined. If you do it right, it will enable your really good builders and these small teams to build that second bucket — things people haven't seen before. When you have experiences like, in four days, you completely build a new idea that's 80% of the way there, it's so inspiring to people that they actually spend more of their free time and free thought cycles thinking about new ideas. To me, that's one of the most exciting parts of what's happening with AI.

But I also think — for existing companies who have successful customer experiences at scale — if they think about AI as primarily just incrementally improving the experience, they will very likely not have the winning experiences three to five years from now. Every single one of these experiences we know — even the ones that seem the most difficult to imagine changing — are going to be meaningfully different with AI in a few years. If you want to think more than incrementally, you have to find a way to get teams to reimagine from scratch what those applications look like if you were building them today with all the new technology available.

Alexa: The Brains Had to Be Rewired

In Alexa, I felt like it was fairly obvious that we had to do that. The brains of Alexa were really inventive at the time it was built, but the capabilities of what the brains could be were so different because of generative AI that you had to rewire the brains of Alexa if you wanted to provide a great customer experience and be relevant over a long period of time.

Even though it was fairly obvious, it was difficult. Teams are connected to what they've built and proud of what they've built, with hard-earned scars on the tenets of what works and doesn't work. To try to get teams to completely start over and reimagine takes time, because teams will say, "That's not how we've done it. We've tried that and it hasn't worked."

The Harder Case

What's harder is to take experiences — our retail business, Prime Video, Fire TV, Prime Music — where it's not as obvious that the technology has a much better solution today. But I actually believe every single one of those businesses, we need to reinvent. We have teams of people working on versions of those businesses today that are totally reimagined. Will we get it right from the get-go? Probably not. We'll find ways to iterate our way into it. But it's already yielding all sorts of new ideas and customer experiences that we think are very compelling.

Then what will be interesting is the race between: do you want a completely different experience that's like something like a new app almost? Or do those advance quickly enough that you add them into the existing experience, where you end up meaningfully changing the overall customer experience bit by bit over the next couple of years as you find elements that work? But I do think every one of these experiences has to be different in the next few years if you want to be a successful leader.

It reminds me of when I first began my career as an engineer — my boss said, "Everything is up for discussion until the first line of code is written, and then it's religious."

By the way, with the customers too — you're going to have some big set of customers that loves the current experience. Every single big transformation, almost — maybe you have some examples that aren't — is a huge change. The technology and the product and the customer experience and the business elements have to be compelling enough to want to change. But then when that's true, it doesn't just happen. It's a huge change management.

Moving from on-premises to the cloud is the same type of transition. Lots of infrastructure leaders were really proud of what they built, and they knew it inside and out, and they were in the middle of the action, and they didn't want to learn something new. It's going to be the same thing with trying to reinvent all your customer experiences. We're all proud of what we've built over the last 10 years, and we all have a hundred things that could make them better that we're excited about and spend all our waking hours working on. To think about how do I completely start over — intellectually and emotionally, it's hard to do.

Advice to an 18-Year-Old in 2026

We just incubated the Horowitz and Andreessen Academy a few weeks ago to help young people prepare for this transformation. You've said how AI makes building easier, but young people still need to learn real expertise. If you were 18 in 2026, what advice would you have for yourself?

I have a 25- and a 22-year-old. The 22-year-old was 19 when this was starting to really take off. I learned very quickly that you can't tell them not to use AI in education — that ship has left the station, that train has left the station. I think universities would be wise not to fight it. It's a tool that people are going to use.

And yet at the same time, I think all young people — and for us, we have a lot of people (we have a writing culture) who are using AI to write — you can tell when something's been written by AI. The pieces aren't put together quite right.

So the advice I would give somebody young — and I gave my kids — was: you can't run away from it, and you can't wish it away. It's going to be incredibly impactful in your life, in every experience that you try and use, in your work. It will allow you to invent in ways that just weren't possible for us before it. So you really need to learn about it. You need to educate yourself about it. You need to use it a lot. You need to try doing things that are outside of your comfort zone. Neither of my kids were developers, but they have used AI to build applications and use it as kind of the focal point of how you operate your day and how you use tools at work.

But Not a Replacement for Critical Reasoning

I don't think it replaces critical reasoning and thinking. This is true for universities. If I think about business school as an example — you would get these three cases that you had to analyze every day. You had to do a lot of reading, you had to take notes, you had to figure out what the key issues were, then you got all these exhibits and you took notes on those, and then you had to put together what you thought the plan should be for that company. Oftentimes there were a bunch of people who just didn't do the work — didn't do the reading or the research or the note-taking. And all that kind of goes away with AI.

AI is going to be able to get everybody to that advanced starting spot much more quickly. But I would also say that the actual putting the dots and the pieces together — either to build a strategy, or an approach, or a plan, or a new product, or a new customer experience — I don't think AI is going to do that for most people most of the time. It's not that it'll never happen. I still think you're going to need human judgment, ingenuity, invention, and experimentation, and thinking about how all the pieces come together, to end up building amazing experiences and businesses. You want to use the tools — they're going to be huge aids — but I still think critical reasoning and thinking is going to be very important in everything we do.

Closing: Three Transformations at Once

You guys are in businesses as diverse as satellite connectivity, robotics, healthcare. The ambition is incredible to think this business started as selling books on the internet. How do you make sense of the vast range — and how do you avoid spreading yourself too thin?

I'd say a few things. First, I think we are living in an era of three of the biggest transformations in our lifetime, and maybe ever: between AI, robotics, and space development. They're all huge, and they all are going to completely change a number of customer experiences we all encounter.

We are in the middle of all three of those big transformations. Look at what we're doing in our retail business and how we use robotics; what we're doing on the AI side, both in making it easier for internal and external builders to build successful AI applications and agents, as well as reinventing all our consumer experiences; if you think about Amazon Leo — our low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation we're building for the 500 million households around the world that don't have broadband connectivity. There's an incredible set of transformations happening that we have a chance to help customers leverage in a way that makes their lives better, and that leads to long-term sustainable businesses for ourselves as well.

I think we have a chance to be much more relevant in helping customers across many more areas. I'm not even mentioning what we're doing in grocery, in autonomous driving / ride-hailing, in healthcare.

"Spreading Too Thin": A Different View

We've often had this internal debate — and a lot of external folks have asked the same question — "What's being spread too thin?"

I think some of that depends on a combination of how you organize yourself and what you're willing to invest. Because we don't try to have the same group of people manage multiple businesses, and we organize in this decentralized, single-threaded way: if you have the right leaders and the right builders on those teams, and you have an experience that if it's big enough could move the needle, and you have a differentiated idea, and a space that is not being that well served — you have the opportunity to pursue a lot of these things simultaneously. We have, over a long period of time.

It just comes down to how much you're willing to invest. There are some companies, very understandably, who say, "We're going to stick to our knitting. We're going to stick to the core business we have and we're going to grow that." That, by the way, can be a very successful strategy. And we are very intent on our existing businesses continuing to grow — I think we've done so pretty successfully, at a good clip. But there are so many other customer experiences that we know customers really want us to help solve, that we can — that are going to help our customers and change our business long-term. We'll keep pursuing those.

That's an inspiring note to end on — sort of endless ambition. Andy, thanks so much for coming on the podcast.

Yeah, thank you, Andy. Thank you for having me. I appreciate it, guys.

### 1. 这不是三次独立战略，是同一个剧本演了三遍
Jassy 这场访谈里最被忽略的事实是：他正在用**同一套剧本**跑第三轮，而几乎没有人识别出这个模式。
- **2001–2003**：内部基础设施痛点 → 诞生 AWS - **2022**：履约网络过度建设 → 区域化重构 → 速度与成本双降 - **2024–2026**：AI 算力稀缺 → 垂直整合 + 2200 亿美元 CapEx
而最微妙的证据藏在 Annapurna 这桩收购里。Jassy 亲口承认：**他们当年不是为了 AI 芯片而买的 Annapurna**，最初只是想做一张虚拟化网卡（NIC），把服务器"几乎 100% 让给计算"。但同一个团队后来做出了 Graviton，又做出了 Tranium。换句话说，Annapurna 是一个被买下的"**芯片期权**"——Jassy 当年并不知道未来需要什么芯片，但他知道自己需要**一个可被反复召唤的芯片团队**。十年后这个期权兑现为对抗 Nvidia 的筹码。这是教科书级别的"可选性资产（optionality asset）"投资，但以收购形态呈现，让大多数

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、所有故事其实是同一个故事：体育"中产阶级"的塌陷与"金融提取层"的降临

表面看，本期节目在讨论四件不相关的事——WTA 的财务困境、LIV Golf 2.0、因凡蒂诺的政治求生、法甲的媒体权崩塌。但把它们放在同一张桌子上，你会看到同一个系统性现象的四副面孔：一层"金融提取层"正在体育产业的中间层上方悄悄凝固。真正的游戏已经不在球场上，而是在税法条款、永续权利金、NOL（净营业亏损）结转和 DTC 替代曲线里。

  • CVC 用 1.5 亿美元换 WTA 20% 永续商业权益；
  • BC Partners 用 3 亿美元债务工具，试图锁定 LIV 高达 50 亿美元的 NOL 税盾——相当于以折扣价购买未来 10 亿美元的企业所得税抵免；
  • Avenue Capital 用 3.2 亿欧元买意甲国际版权 10%（永续）；
  • UEFA 的"团结付款"则是用联赛收入内横向转移，把 PSG、拜仁、尤文强行留在"顶级俱乐部"的角色里。

让人意外的观察：所有被"救助"的组织都以为自己拿到了资金——但本质上，它们正在把自己转化成一种税务工具、永续现金流资产或政治工具。资本方的真正回报根本不在这项运动是否兴旺上。这就是为什么 BC Partners 派出的是债券基金经理（Ted Goldthorpe），而不是股权投资合伙人。

二、BC Partners × LIV 的真正本质：制药业的"税务倒置"被搬进了高尔夫球场

Pat 对 BC 结构的拆解是本期最重要的技术性洞见，但他没有把这个模式和一个更宽的图景连起来。

跨领域连接：BC Partners 对 LIV 的操作，本质是一种"损失收割（loss harvesting）"。这种玩法在以下几个产业早就是标准动作： - 大型制药公司的"税务倒置"：以收购爱尔兰壳公司的方式降低有效税率； - 美国地方报业的私募股权收购（Alden Global Capital、Gannett）：接盘亏损报纸，不是为了做新闻，是为了抽离房地产与压低劳动力； - 加密货币寒冬里的"NOL 猎人"：2022–2024 年专门以极低对价收购破产加密公司，为的是把它们的净营业亏损用在其他赛道的利润上。

Dean Burmeister 那段关于"kids and rhinos"的采访之所以令人毛骨悚然，是因为他正在无意识地扮演制药公司代言人：讲一个关于使命的温情故事，让观众忽略背后其实是精密的财务工程。Pat 感到"slightly distasteful" 的那一刻，其实隐约闻到了ESG 式话术首次大规模入侵职业高尔夫的味道——道德叙事成了税务结构的糖衣。

三、FIFA 的真正统治者不是因凡蒂诺，是迈克尔·里基茨

Sephrin 失败的表层原因是"没趁热打铁"。但真正的深层原因是：他误读了 FIFA 的权力地理学。

当牙买加足协主席 Michael Ricketts 坦白"this is about the cash"——4000 万美元比道德立场重要——他不是在腐败，而是在精准表达一个被欧洲长期低估的政治集团的理性偏好：加勒比 + 非洲 + 亚洲小国。这个集团手握不成比例的 FIFA 投票权。Montigulani 之所以退出竞选，是因为他发现连 Concacaf 内部的小岛国都不买他的账——而这些小岛国名义上在他治下。

跨领域连接：这个结构与联合国大会的投票政治几乎同构。欧洲永远以为自己掌握着"道德话语权"，但联大上的小国集团早已学会用投票换基础设施——这正是中国"一带一路"外交的核心机制之一。因凡蒂诺本质上在 FIFA 内部运行着一个微缩版的"全球南方外交体系"：他发给小国的世界杯分成，就是他的 BRI。

Sephrin 以为自己在对抗一个腐败对手；他真正面对的，是一套替代性的全球治理体系。他输，是因为他从未真正理解自己在和什么对抗。而 UEFA 现在转向"法律途径"，是典型的欧洲式回退——当政治牌打不开时，去诉诸规则。但他们将再次发现：规则本身也是政治的产物。

四、把四段故事缝合在一起的那条隐线：在关键时刻的集体精神退缩

节目开场，Pat 嘲弄 Charlie 的"reverse Kirsty"——需要被打一巴掌才能上场。如果你带着这只耳朵听完整期，会发现每一个失败案例的本质都是同一种精神退缩：

  • Sephrin 本来攻势正盛，却在关键一拳收了半力；
  • WTA 主席明知财务模型不可持续，却不敢对球员说真话；
  • LIV 的律师在法庭上大声宣称"球员自由是我们的基石"——所有人都知道这是弥天大谎，但没人敢当面戳穿；
  • 法甲俱乐部明知自己已经不是顶级联赛，却集体拒绝完成心理哀悼；
  • John Rahm 为什么能走？因为他敢于把 1 亿美元无担保债权一次性清掉——他是整期节目里唯一一个真正做出"硬选择"的人物。

最让人意外的转折：Charlie 和 Pat 自己也在同一个模式里。他们自嘲"没人比我们更喝 LIV 的 Kool-Aid"，"别人都不聊 LIV 了只有我们还在聊"——这段自嘲其实无意中暴露了体育商业评论的最大结构性偏差：评论者与被评论对象共享同一种"再给一次机会"的乐观偏见；他们用"下周我们再看看"的节奏，推迟一个早就该做出的终局判断。

这就是本期播客真正的"啊哈时刻"：在体育资本主义的末端游戏里，真正敢说"结束了"的声音，永远来自圈外。圈内权威——无论是球员、主席、投资人，还是评论员——都因为生计、情感或叙事惯性，被困在"再等一下"的集体幻觉里。John Rahm 之所以显得突兀，是因为他做了一件圈内人几乎不会做的事：他不等了。

WTA 的财务迷局：Valerie Camo 的"同酬使命"

Should we crack on with the podcast that I sent you — out of interest, from the WTA?

Yes, from the chairwoman, I think, of the WTA — Valerie Camo. She went on the Andy Roddick podcast Served. It was just interesting for us because we had speculated a couple of weeks ago about the WTA's finances — because it had become apparent during the US Open tennis, during presentations that were made to players and their agents at that time, that the cash balance of the WTA at the end of this year was likely to fall as low as $15 million, and that during the course of 2026 it looked like they were going to have lost on an operational basis $25 to $30 million — having taken in $150 million of third-party investment from CVC four years ago, which is being paid out annually in tranches of $30 million. The last tranche of $30 million is next year, 2027.

So we were speculating about what does this actually look like? Basically what's happened is that all of this extra money that's been taken in has been sprayed around on increasing pay levels. We were not very optimistic about the idea of using capital investment to boost prize money before revenues are able to afford it. We weren't absolutely sure that's what had happened, or indeed that the equal prize money was necessarily the one driving force, but we speculated that that looked as if it were the case.

And Valerie Camo came on this podcast of Andy Roddick and said: 100% our main target, our main focus, is equal prize money. That's the entire point of the WTA — was founded to achieve equal prize money.

Which I think is just so odd. Right? Now, everyone knows the foundation story of the WTA — Billie Jean King in the 1960s, turning up for a tournament, I think it was in Italy, and the men were being paid five times as much as she was being paid to be there, and she resented that and thought: "We need to get together, we need to form a women's tour."

So yeah, it's true that in the foundation story there is a recognition of the fact that men were being paid in a different universe to what women were being paid at the time. But I don't think it's the case really that the entire foundation of the WTA is simply to achieve equal prize money.

Prize money is an outcome. Prize money is a sort of end goal, and it may even be a very laudatory part of your objectives — your stretch objectives over a protracted period of time. But to basically say "my job as chairman, my main job as chairman is to achieve equal pay" is odd — unless you understand the job as fundamentally answering to the players.

And what became clear during this interview — she referred in several places to the fact that fundamentally her bosses are her players. Now, this is a strange situation because effectively the players are the players of today. They're not the players of yesterday and they're not the players of tomorrow. So on a normal circumstance, you'd assume that whoever's running the WTA would think: "Okay, I had to balance the priorities here. I have to think about the players of today and do the best I possibly can. But at the same time, I also have to think about the players of tomorrow as well, because what we can't do is mortgage the future to make the current players happy."

And yet that is exactly what has happened. They have taken in $150 million worth of investment from CVC in return for 20% of their ongoing commercial rights. So effectively they're promising away the future in order to pile up cash today — and all in the pursuit of equal pay today. Not equal pay on a gradual basis as revenues support it. No, equal pay today, even though revenues do not support it.

— Cash for the five years from the start of when CVC invested, but it's equity dividends in perpetuity. — Exactly. — Right. So in other words, those who play now, you get benefits from the cash. Those of you that are going to play in 10 years, you'll actually have money taken away unless we can find another way to generate the money to put into the prize pool. — Right. And that was what was interesting.

Right? And look, I think I've got to grant some latitude when people use these types of shorthands. I don't want to hold them to every single — you know, be arsey about it and saying, "Well, it's not exactly like the Super Bowl." But let's reflect on the fact: it really is not like the Super Bowl.

Here's a key difference. What is the pinnacle of NFL? The Super Bowl. What is the pinnacle of tennis? Grand slams. This is a core, core difference. It cannot be the Super Bowl because it's not the thing which the whole year leads up to.

她的叙述 vs. 她的数学

I just want to read out — because it shows you the position that women's tennis actually is in — when she was describing the strength of it, she says:

"We have more opportunity than any other women's sport and some of the men's. We are the only women's sport that is truly global. One-name superstar athletes known all over the world. We aren't a startup. We're the legacy. We have the most powerful deep fan base — balance between men and women. Take all of this together and layer the integration with the men's game. You put all of that together and who has it better than us? Why shouldn't we be ambitious?"

Now, no one would argue against that. Where it starts to lose its weight is when she says "fiscal discipline is our ambition." When she says that — "my background is financial and strategic" — and then on the flip side you come out and make a statement which really surprised me. It was kind of quite loose, but it was: "other sports have had to prove and then get" — and she was referring to prize money, i.e. as if saying "you said to me the cart comes before the horse here; most people have to prove it."

Yeah, but I mean that's what business is. You don't go and get a big shiny office before you can afford the rent. You don't hire a market-leading CEO before you can pay the salary. In these situations, there just seems to be that disconnect of: your business doesn't justify the means of your spend.

You're starting off — all serious sports industry commentators are starting off — from a different position from her. We are making the assumption that the number one priority of sports business is to create something which is sustainable, growing, pays prize money out of its revenues, blah blah blah. But she's not. She's starting from the position of saying, "Oh, that's all great. That's all fine. I get that. But my number one priority is paying the women as much as the men get, even though we've got half the revenues."

Now if you start off from that position, effectively what she then has to do is retrofit a strategy to achieve something which is non-negotiable. And that is how it came across in this thing — which is that in taking the job, she has had it made clear to her by the players: it is non-negotiable that you achieve equal prize money. It is your job to achieve equal prize money.

对 WTA 主席，是否该抱有同情？

Do you have any sympathy? Can I just quickly ask that — because she then went on to talk about the lack of inventory really that they have to work with. We discussed this last week and we said look, at some stage, if the players want that equal prize money, the players are going to have to maybe take a bit of a commercial hit, because they are going to need to package some form of rights up to allow the tour to sell them, so that they can make more money commercially as a tour.

Six out of 10 of the top paid players, men and women — Forbes said — are women. In that stat, men are making most of their money on the court; women are making most of their money off the court. So women are getting fantastic pay from brands and commercial partners. And then they want on-the-court to match it. Whereas the men on the court are making a lot of money because the tour is generating more money, but they may not be as commercially viable across the board as a lot of the women are.

Charlie, you asked me a question. Do I feel some sympathy for her? And the answer is no.

First of all, she's agreed to take the job. Secondly, she has decided not to do the thing that real leaders do, which is tell some uncomfortable truths. And the uncomfortable truth to tell here is: "Look, if you're asking me to achieve equal prize money, I can do that with your support" — this is talking to the players — "okay? If what you're saying is that you want to max out yourself on your own personal commercial income, and that on top of that you want me to achieve equal prize money with the men based off an inventory which is basically tiny — which is the Tour Finals plus some brand sponsorship for the tour as a whole, but where those brands aren't getting access to the players because the players already signed their rights away to other sponsors themselves personally — I'm sorry, that's not achievable."

So if you really believe in what Billie Jean believed in — start pooling your own. Put your own money where your mouth is. But they don't want to do that. They want to have their cake and eat it. They want to be able to be much better paid in sponsorship terms than the men and then also equally paid in terms of the prize money. And there isn't the money there to pay for it.

Which brings us back to the Tour Finals and the "Super Bowl of women's sport." When she was asked what do you mean by that, she's like, "Well, obviously the tournament itself, but then we're also going to have a fanfest." So it's a sort of copycat of what Craig Tiley did in Australia with the Australian Open. "And we're going to have a women's sport conference." Right? Well, the women's sport conference won't butter much toast commercially. That will be at best a break-even type thing. Worthy, no doubt, but a break-even type thing. And the FanFest — well, let's see. Let's see what that looks like commercially. But I somewhat doubt that that is going to be the thing which turns this into effectively being able to replace the money that CVC's been pumping in.

Because that's what's going to have to happen here — the $30 million a year that CVC's been putting in is going to have to be replaced. And effectively from listening to that podcast, it is going to have to be replaced by revenue generated mostly from the Tour Finals. Which — if she pulls it off, and if that Tour Finals event ends up making $30 million bucks profit a year and that's able to replace the CVC money, notwithstanding the fact that 20% of the future's been promised away but leave that to one side — then I think I'd have to stand back and say: wow, what a job she would have done.

So I'm not saying that it can't be done. I'm saying that I think it would be better for sports leaders to front up to the reality of the challenge to their stakeholders. Doesn't mean say so you don't go on and try and achieve it. You can still have stretch targets, you can still have ambitions, as she puts it, but taking it as read that that's definitely going to happen when effectively your bank balance is currently at zero strikes me as a massive risk.

And I do think the WTA Tour Finals can be — let me be quite clear — can be better, bigger, bolder than it currently is. Yes. Do I think it will be? Yes, I do. Having it in a big serious sports city like Charlotte as opposed to in Riyadh — do I think that's infinitely better? Yes. Do I think they'll get much bigger crowds? Yes. Do I think they'll get bigger TV audiences? Yes. Do I think they'll get more mainline sponsors? Definitely yes. So that's not the question. The question is: there's a $30 to $40 million a year hole here which needs filling. Do I think that that's the sole answer to that? Bit more skeptical.

BC Partners 真正在做什么：债 vs. 股，与 NOL 税盾

I just want to ask you one other question, Charlie. Since you have a sort of financial fund management side to your life — Ted Goldthorpe, this guy from BC Partners, is a debt partner there, which is to say that he invests money as debt. This feels to me like under normal circumstances this would be an equity investment. And yet the fact that it's Ted Goldthorpe from BC Partners suggests that it's a debt investment. How does that work? How can you — because equity value is not non-existent, right?

Okay. Well, do you remember we were kind of laughing about this? We were joking. Do you remember when the news first came out? We said this cannot be an equity play. There has to be another financial motive — with very intelligent people running various types of financial institutions recognizing an opportunity to gain some value off the misfortune of LIV Golf and/or the people that have been left on the shelf.

So what do you think Ted's doing?

The point is that they have recognized that off the losses that LIV Golf made — $5 billion — that presents a significant opportunity for them to gain some tax exemptions in the future. So they're $5 billion in net operating losses, as they call it. And this is where it gets technical. So trying to keep it simple for myself and everyone else:

You can offset those net operating losses — the taxes associated with future profits that you make in your portfolio — against net operating losses in other ventures that you're involved in. So governments traditionally did this to try and remove some of the distress on struggling businesses, to give them an opportunity to recover. Private equity has been taking advantage of this because they know they can front cash to get companies out of situations, and what they want to do is look at their broader portfolio and say: right, so in this case, if BC and its sports portfolio — it kind of wants to run a CVC-type model — let's say they made $5 billion in profits over the next few years. They could offset the corporate tax — corporate income tax, which is about 20% — they could offset $1 billion of that against the $5 billion losses that would be associated with LIV's debt currently. I.e., they pay no tax.

Right? So effectively the deal here — and this answers really well a question that's been lurking ever since I saw Ted's face, thinking "what the hell is a debt guy doing in this?" — I'm looking at it, thinking, okay, so what you're basically saying is that BC Partners is potentially buying $5 billion of tax credits — which nets out at $1 billion, cuz it's 20% — effectively $1 billion of tax credits in return for $300 million of debt.

It looks like that, right? Drip-feeding this money in as well most likely. So, you know, I think it's $50 million. They put $4 million up at the beginning to cover some of the bankruptcy. I think that could extend to $50 million.

I then think — and I'm not sure, but I think — these challenges they've got now around when they can pull out: if certain players aren't signed, or if they don't get to the stage they need to to continue, they can pull that money. No more than $50 million would be committed. If they do get to the stage, then the $300 million is still on the table. But absolutely, from what it looks like, the real value to BC Partners is for the money that they can save in the future on a broader sports portfolio by offsetting the taxes of any future profits on their other businesses.

Now, if you look at it like that, then it's a good deal for them. What's not to like?

And that explains a lot. But then what we don't want to see — and I think where you have the challenge, and where we know golfers have the challenge — is: don't sit on a panel and spin it to us as a "$100 million equity investment and an opportunity for players" who are sitting there facing massive losses because they've had to convert their cash into equity if they want anything to do with this. This is why I find it a bit distasteful.

Because some players, particularly golfers, actually are quite smart. But some are not, and some can be easily taken in — and these are years of their life which are the critical earning years. And these people in some cases should be going off and making their career back again on the main tours, qualifying for majors, cementing legacies and all this type of stuff. And you've got slightly slimy, slick-suited Americans sitting on panels at sports conferences talking about how this is going to be this amazing new equity play and the players are so lucky to be involved — when in actual fact is ultimately potentially — and I must say potentially because we don't know — but it's potentially a piece of financial structuring really, where if it does come off great, but if it doesn't come off then BC Partners win anyway.
