But anything that relies on having a suitable candidate to go up against Infantino at this stage, I think is crazy thinking and a waste of their time. It has to be about: can you remove this man from power in a — by the sounds of it — legal way, which makes that position completely untenable for him. Not in the eyes of public opinion, but in some form of law. If that's the card he's playing, fair enough.

I don't know, Charlie. I look at this and I see our Italian friend sitting there gleaming into his final term as president in April.

— An Italian friend of mine got very offended when I said he was Italian. He said he's Swiss. And I said, "Well, he was born in Italy to Italian parents, but yes, he is currently categorized…" — It's funny how we have that.

But yes — I mean, as I said, when money at this level is involved in developing nations in a football economy that…

— You think Čeferin fumbled the ball basically. — Yeah. And after such incredible — he had momentum, didn't he? Momentum and linguistic power. We spoke about the Alastair Campbell interview. And it was around that time, wasn't it? That was around a few weeks after the World Cup, when the whole FFE thing had come out, and when the wind was in Čeferin's sails, and Montagliani seemed to have Concacaf onside. Basically, you're saying that he should have pressed right there and right then: "Infantino has to go, otherwise European countries are out of all FIFA competitions indefinitely."

I think if you're the ruthless leader that needs the result that he needed, then yes, I get it. I get why — because playing the diplomatic game is the right one. But if you feel as strongly as he did and the language — remember the language that was being used was so strong — to then not act in the most strong way…

— So you're basically saying ultimately he was all hat and no cattle. — Yeah. — Well, let's see — let's just see in case he's got something up his sleeve.

法甲与意甲：欧洲"中间市场"的塌陷

Right. Moving on. You thought — and I agree with you — that it was time to have a look at the French football league, and connectedly potentially Serie A, the Italian top division as well.

What prompted that thought from you?

I've seen a couple of articles in the last week with the dramatic headlines, something along the lines of "every owner in France wants to sell" — obviously with a caveat against PSG. So you go and have a look in these articles and you base what information they're sharing with the conversations that we've had previously: i.e. the collapse of the French media rights landscape, meaning that clubs have lost a huge — well, that their core revenue stream, the direct-to-consumer model that's come out the back of it not really working, French clubs relying on selling players to generate almost all of their revenue operationally. Knowing a few owners in there basically saying "if it's Champions League or bust for us." And when that kind of compounded, and you start looking at the viability of some of these leagues long-term — not in single seasons but long-term — you start to really question: if there is this existential risk to top-level football in Europe, as these leagues get weaker, the Premier League and English football gets stronger because they're sweeping up a lot of the money that has been spent in these leagues from media, broadcast, etc.

You'll talk to this, 'cuz you made a very good point to me earlier, but it just prompted me to think that amongst all of this, I think we should have a discussion about it because I don't think anyone else has really been going into some of this. And I think it's become a casual, almost throwaway comment that French football's in trouble. But some of these numbers really — and we look at a lot of numbers — they really made me, for want of a better phrase…

法甲的实际数字

So last year, Ligue 1 and Ligue Deux had a net loss of €542 million, which was double what it did the year before. The operating loss before player sales was €1.4 billion. The profit on player sales was €886 million.

So if you hadn't had those player sales, that league lost nearly €1.5 billion. Now that's a worry in itself. You can't sell €886 million worth of talent every single year. You may be able to sell a few hundred million's worth of talent, but you can't rely on it as a core. Also, Paris was €333 million of that. Oh, sorry — PSG share of Ligue 1 revenue is 40%.

Yeah. So what has been happening here?

Everyone knows that, in quotation marks, French Ligue lost their TV deal. And what that means basically is that they used to get paid around about £500 million a year by Canal Plus, the main cable pay TV provider — Sky Sports equivalent I think — in France. Canal Plus pulled out of that in a midstay dispute with Ligue. Ligue said, "That's okay because we're going to sell our rights to DAZN," who bought them I think for $450 million. So not far off, same sort of ballpark. After a year or a year and a half, DAZN then pulled out of that contract — and did so in a way which was legally quite nifty, even if not particularly ethical in my view — and they walked away.

The French Ligue then could not find anybody else to take their TV rights. So they went DTC, which is direct-to-consumer, which is forming their own channel where you basically have to subscribe as a football fan to the Ligue channel in order to be able to watch Ligue 1 games domestically in France — out of which they made about €150 million.

So they've gone from a deal with Canal Plus that was paying them 500, to a DTC thing paying — well, getting 150 in revenue. But don't forget they have the cost of production as well. So it's not going to be 150 net; it's going to be 150 gross, out of which the clubs might receive 120. They then get a small amount of money for their foreign rights — I can't remember the exact number but it's 60, 70, 80, 90 something like that. So they're getting about 200 million in total. Hence why between 18 of them they're getting about 10 million each post-costs.

Okay, so that's what's happened.

Roger Mitchell 的宏观判断：欧洲 Pay TV 的"剧目重排"

But what's happening — because what's happening here is also happening in Italy. And as so often when thinking about continental TV rights, I turn to our old friend Roger Mitchell to give me a read on what's happening behind the scenes, because he often understands what's happening with the TV rights negotiations and the movement of different contracts very well.

And what he said was really interesting. He said the macro here is that the domestic sports pay TV providers in countries generally — not just talking about France, not just talking about Italy, we're also talking about Belgium, we're talking about other countries which are non-top-tier countries — those domestic pay TV providers have worked out that they will access the necessary football eyeballs paying subscriptions within their own market by screening the Champions League and the Premier League, and that they will pay much less for the combined Champions League and Premier League than they have been used to paying for their domestic league — for the same amount of eyeballs, if not more.

So this is what happened in France, and it's really interesting when you look at it. Canal Plus used to pay €500 million for Ligue 1. Now they pay €450 million for the combined Champions League and Premier League. And they're not interested in the domestic league anymore. Proving Roger's point — saying that Canal Plus have done the numbers, they're not fools. They've worked out that they are not losing TV subscriptions by no longer televising the domestic league. If they want the football audience, they do the Champions League and the Premier League.

意甲：下一个倒下的多米诺骨牌？

Now let's have a look and see what's happening in Italy — because this could be the next cab off the rank, as Roger says. But this is how it works.

Sky Italia, which forms the same function as Sky does in this country, used to pay €780 million for Serie A primary rights. Now they pay €200 million for the Champions League, €100 million for the Premier League — so that's €300 million — and €180 million for the Serie A secondary rights. That's a certain number of Serie A matches, because the primary rights holder is DAZN.

— Yeah. So they've gone from being Sky Sports to TNT again. Sorry, for the English audience. — Correct. So that's €480 million in total for their football rights, as against €780 million they were previously paying — all to Serie A.

Right. And who's taken up… so DAZN, our old friends at DAZN, took up the slack. And they are paying €700 million for the primary rights. Don't forget, that is against €780 million that Sky Italia were previously paying. So actually it's a 10% reduction, and when you take into account that was five years subsequent, it's more than that because of inflation etc. But put all that to one side, and that contract is coming up in 2028–2029 — that is the last year of that contract.

Now this is where the rubber hits the road. Because there are two potential routes that happen here. One of which is that DAZN says — as with their French market and their Belgian market — they say, "Do you know what? This isn't working. We're not doing it. We're literally just not doing it." Or the second route is they say, "Well, we do want to do it, but we're the only show in town. Sky Italia ain't coming back in for you guys. They've already got themselves tied up with the Premier League, the Champions League, and your secondary rights. So they're not going to come in for your primary rights as well. We're the only show in town. We're not going to pay you 700. We're going to pay you 500."

That's what we're staring down the barrel of here: it could be nothing, or it could be 500, but it sure as hell ain't going to be 700. I'd be amazed if it's going to be 700. I was at a conference recently when a representative of DAZN was saying, "Look, overall we need to manage our rights payments downwards." You and I have mentioned before how enormous their rights liabilities are, and given that they could be potentially IPOing in the next year or two, it's only sensible for them to think about rationalizing their rights payments downwards a bit — preferably a lot, but certainly a bit.

意甲的回应：拉"WTA 把手"

So how are they trying to offset some of this risk? I've got a risk going on — and it's not even a risk, it's like, I would say, a racing certainty. Having already seen a bump down in their rights, they're going to see another bump down. Maybe not quite as dramatic as France, but still a significant bump down.

So they're reaching for, dare I say it, the WTA lever.

— Oh, when will they learn, Charlie? — And this is not a good lever.

For those who have tuned in a little bit late or weren't listening to the bit on tennis earlier on because you're not interested in tennis: the WTA took in $150 million of "quote investment" from CVC in return for CVC having 20% of their commercial rights in perpetuity. And Charlie and I have long said that was a terrible deal. Short-term cash spunked on prize money to give away 20% of your future.

What are Serie A doing, Charles? Look, they're looking to sell 10% of the international rights package in perpetuity to private equity for a single sum which has been valued across different bids slightly differently. But €320 million for 10% is one bid. €650 million for 17% is another bid.

The mathematics are right. So basically they're currently receiving €250 million a year for their international rights.

So is there an argument here that actually Serie A is doing something quite sensible — which is that whilst their foreign rights are still worth something, they're getting some cash in for them to slightly derisk the possibility that actually they don't really go anywhere? Because a valuation of 3.2 billion on your foreign rights when you're currently only getting 250 million a year, and when there's no obvious indication they're about to boom — you know, from a purely mathematical perspective, could that be a good — ?

Yes, but my question is: what is that money going to be used for? That's the key.

Look, in theory, was the WTA taking $150 million of CVC money a bad decision? Not necessarily. You could put a strong argument together for both sides of it. What was a bad decision was putting the $150 million into increasing prize money — i.e. not increasing the overall value of the proposition.

We've talked about CVC putting money into La Liga. That was ring-fenced to ensure that it was spent in certain ways which CVC and La Liga thought would grow the overall value of the proposition. It couldn't just be going and spent on a nice shiny new striker.

Normally when these deals happen, incredibly, money hasn't been ring-fenced. It hasn't been segmented. So leagues and whatever have just run around and spent it however they wish.

One of the deals on the table looks like a very good deal to me. One of them less so. Avenue Capital, which is Marc Lasry's private equity business (Marc Lasry — one of the PGA Enterprises investors, one of the great lads, come back on that — and former Milwaukee Bucks owner), they have a deal reportedly on the table: €320 million for 10%. So values the whole international rights package at €3.2 billion. Is plain equity. So there's no guarantees on future cash flows. It is an equity play, meaning they see value that can be traded later on if the value of the overall proposition increases. That to me looks like a really good deal.

The other deal — for Serie A, yeah. Not so for Avenue. The other bid, which is €650 million, so more money up front, for roughly 17% — values it slightly higher at €3.7 billion but it does come with commitments to pay them on future cash flows. I.e., they will be taking money out in perpetuity. Now look, even that may be a good deal if the money is being put to the right use. €650 million is a lot of money, but I would be more inclined to take that Avenue Capital deal — try and use the €320 million.

And that is the favorite, right? Apparently that is what they're looking to do. They are kind of the preferred bidder, whatever.

Do you think that's a good deal? In theory, financially, economically, yes. In practice, in terms of using it to top up payments to clubs in the short run to try and fill leaky buckets — no. Because that all disappears very quickly, and it puts off the day of reckoning when clubs in Serie A have to cut their cloth to the reality of their situation rather than pretend that they are still in a major European league.

It's also not a lot of money each, is it? Really — €16 million euros each dividing. It'll probably disappear in two seasons. I'm guessing one or two seasons.

大图景：媒体资本从法甲、意甲向英超与欧冠的大迁移

I just want to go back onto the French league and relatedly the Italian league — because what you're actually seeing here is a reallocation of media capital from the French and Italian leagues to the Premier League and the Champions League. That's what's driving the whole thing here.

And that in turn is being driven by effectively algorithmic study — which basically said, right, "If we do this then we get more subscribers; if we do that, we get fewer subscribers." So that is the brutal market, because the broadcasters have got so smart now at judging what does bring eyeballs, what doesn't bring eyeballs, what does lead people to keep their subscriptions, what doesn't — all that type of stuff. They've become really, really good at it.

— One of the reasons why DAZN was pulling out of the deals. It was — — The reason. Yeah. Which is they went into these deals, paid quite a lot of money for them, and then found out there weren't any subscribers there. Well, weren't enough subscribers there to make their financial model work. "Oh, we've got to get out." Right.

So this is almost like a sort of peak globalization point, isn't it? Which is: the rich and the big get richer and bigger — being UEFA and the Premier League — and then the secondary and tertiary products are regarded as fundamentally being non-essential. And become effectively, gradually free-to-air, or else very niche subscription.

And the worst thing — those secondary leagues then consolidate the power of the Premier League. Because you know what the summer showed — I mentioned the talent being the key revenue driver for France. Where do they sell to? They sell to the Premier League. So France now needs the richness, the riches of the Premier League to be able to fund the main part of their business model — for the stats that they're the number one net seller.

The wealth of the Premier League is being funded by these domestic leagues' own markets. That's a humiliating thing. Exactly. And then those markets are relying on that money spent on the Premier League to then pay them in talent.

Indeed. Right. So just on a quick back of a fag packet: French and Italian Premier League TV payments are now €250 million a year. Right. So the Premier League is receiving more from French and Italian punters than the French league is receiving from all of its domestic punters — €150 million. That's how bad things are getting. In fact, the amount that French punters are paying for EPL, which is about €100 million, is not that different to the €150 million they're paying for domestic. They're paying almost as much for the Premier League as they are for the domestic product.

豪门的反应、UEFA 的"团结付款贿赂"

So you want these big teams — your PSG or Juventus — you know, what's your reaction to this? European Super League?

So your short-term reaction, which is what it has been: "We have to pressurize UEFA into giving us guaranteed payments" — which they've done through — what's it called? Solidarity payments. Solidarity. Something like that. Which is basically PSG receiving €70 or €80 million just for being PSG. Just for being PSG. And that effectively is UEFA's current bribe to be able to enable a very small number of clubs from these leagues to be able to dine at the top table with the Premier League clubs is basically bungs from UEFA.

The problem is UEFA can't stop giving the same — well, giving payments to Premier League clubs as well. Has to be done on a sort of roughly equal basis. The Premier League clubs get a bit less because it's a more competitive league, so there are more clubs for it to be paid out to. Whereas if you are PSG or Bayern or Juve or Milan, whatever it might be, then you can get more.

But fundamentally that is what's going on here. UEFA are propping up a small number of European clubs against the Premier League, to get around the fact that their domestic revenues have been cannibalized by the Premier League and indeed the Champions League, as it happens.

It's just a really interesting trend. And a worrying trend, right?

— Well, worrying for whom? The domestic market. — What you're seeing here is you're seeing the Premier League's revenues becoming more and more broad-based, which means they have less and less individual risk on any one contract. So it's great if you're the Premier League. It's great if you're English football. Because if you're — it's great if you're the Championship. You know, we've talked about the value of the leagues within this from a viewership perspective — as the third most viewed league in Europe, the Championship.

Look, I mean, if the Premier League is just getting bigger — and it will get bigger and bigger and bigger. One of the reasons why City need to get sorted out quick, you know. They're on such an upward trajectory. They're cannibalizing this market. They're getting more money. They're eating off other people's plates. They're eating other people's lunch. Absolutely.

But on the flip side — back to sport and what sport is and why it's so important here that we have payments going down a pyramid. Every country has football that we're talking about here at the heart of much of its social fabric, of its communities. Same discussion, same arguments that we have here. It's a major, major issue for these heritage organizations, these institutions, these fans.

The reason for these enormous losses, Charlie, that you're talking about in the French league is because psychologically the French clubs have not yet got used to — and particularly the French fan bases have not yet got used to — the idea that basically we're just feeding clubs the Premier League. Right. So if you're a Marseille fan and you're supporting one of the great clubs of Europe and there's 60,000 people in the stadium and you have great pride in your club and the way it represents the community and all this type of stuff — and then fundamentally all of your players are just being sold every summer because the revenue is just not there to support playing top players' wages and so on and so forth — they are in open revolt against this stuff.

At so many French clubs, the fans are in open revolt because they cannot understand or accept that their league is no longer one — or maybe the lowest — but one of the top five leagues, is now dropped out of that. It's now dropping down towards Scottish Premiership, Dutch League, Belgian League levels. It's heading in that — in fact, it's much closer to those. In fact, the Portuguese league, even more so.

Its biggest team doesn't take the league seriously. Its biggest team plays its star players for one-third of the games. Right. It has the double European champions in that league, right? Which is another issue — that's another whole issue.

I was listening to an interview with a former senior executive at the French league who said, "Well, you know, in an ideal world, don't let a good crisis go to waste. You could use this moment when French league football is at its absolute lowest point to totally recast the whole league and do something really bold about it." Right? "Let's just say that we want to become the most competitive league in Europe." Yeah — bloody difficult to do when PSG are currently your only sellable product. Right. Very, very hard.

Anyhow, one to keep an eye on, Charles. But thanks for raising it.

结语

— No, not at all. Great discussions. Hey, look, that was a mixed bag today. — It certainly was. — Really plenty to go through. Um, guys, hope you enjoyed it as always. Keep the comments flowing. I'm sure there was plenty in there for you guys to get stuck into. Thank you, Charlie, and we will see you all next week. — Thanks, Charlie.

item.description:
## 一、所有故事其实是同一个故事：体育"中产阶级"的塌陷与"金融提取层"的降临
表面看，本期节目在讨论四件不相关的事——WTA 的财务困境、LIV Golf 2.0、因凡蒂诺的政治求生、法甲的媒体权崩塌。但把它们放在同一张桌子上，你会看到**同一个系统性现象的四副面孔**：一层"金融提取层"正在体育产业的中间层上方悄悄凝固。真正的游戏已经不在球场上，而是在税法条款、永续权利金、NOL（净营业亏损）结转和 DTC 替代曲线里。
- CVC 用 1.5 亿美元换 WTA 20% 永续商业权益； - BC Partners 用 3 亿美元债务工具，试图锁定 LIV 高达 50 亿美元的 NOL 税盾——相当于以折扣价购买未来 10 亿美元的企业所得税抵免； - Avenue Capital 用 3.2 亿欧元买意甲国际版权 10%（永续）； - UEFA 的"团结付款"则是用联赛收入内横向转移，把 PSG、拜仁、尤文强行留在"顶级俱乐部"的角色里。
**让人意外的观察**：所有被"救助"的组织都以为自己拿到了资金——但本质上，**它们正在把自己转化成一种税务工具、永续现金流资产或政治

item.title: [No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups] Democratizing Security for the Agentic Web with CloudFlare CTO Dane Knecht
item.dc:creator: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽略的真相：加密学从未假设攻击者是机器

Dane 轻描淡写提到的那个「用数字 4 作为随机种子」的笑话，其实是整个互联网信任模型的墓志铭。几十年来，密码学的"实用安全"并非建立在数学强度之上，而是建立在攻击者的疲劳曲线之上——没人有耐心逐一尝试几亿次愚蠢的密钥选择。换句话说，我们把人类红队工程师的"注意力稀缺"当作了防御的隐藏基石。

而 agent 不睡觉、不吃饭、不索要加班费。这不是"攻击能力的提升"，而是防御前提的失效。我们突然发现，整个 WebPKI、整个 TLS 生态，都在用一个暗含的假设跑了 25 年：攻击者会在某个时点选择放弃。这个假设刚刚、永久地、不可逆地错了。

一个让人意外的推论：这意味着所有"足够难"的旧东西都要重新定义"足够"——不仅是加密，还有 CAPTCHA、反欺诈的"冷却时间"设计、甚至司法程序里的"合理时间内"概念。只要文明的某一环节曾默认"没人闲到做这件事"，agent 都会把它击穿。

二、"Agent Kitties"：教会与印刷术的 2026 版重演

Dane 顺口说的"不是国家队，是高中生"几乎是采访里被埋没的最大洞见。这不是"攻击民主化"，这是宗教改革的技术版重演。

1517 年马丁·路德之所以能把教会打穿，不是因为他神学更强，而是因为古登堡印刷术让"解读圣经"这件事从神职人员的专属能力变成了识字者的日常。路德甚至没有"颠覆教会"的宏大计划——他只是贴了 95 条论纲。

今天的"agent kitties"也没有颠覆国家网络战的意图。他们只是在参加 CTF，顺便拿点 bug bounty。但当国家级能力的边际成本从"数百名工程师多年研发"降到"一个 16 岁小孩加 Opus 订阅费"时，真正被摧毁的是国家暴力的垄断性优势——这是 1648 年威斯特伐利亚体系之后头一次。

跨领域联系：这与晚清火器扩散如出一辙。清廷不是输给了洋人的坚船利炼，而是输给了火器一旦量产之后国家不再是唯一能行使致命暴力的主体这件事。CFO Dane 乐观地说"人类会团结起来"，但历史上这类技术扩散的终局从不是"大家更团结了"，而是新的权力实体从技术缝隙里长出来。那个实体可能就是 Cloudflare 本身。

三、HTTP 402：互联网最长的"等待室"，和它意外的隐喻

Tim Berners-Lee 在 1989 年协议草案里塞进去的 402 Payment Required，是整个互联网协议栈里沉睡最久的一枚种子——37 年里几乎没人用过。Dane 几乎是以调侃的口气说"x402 又复活了"，但这里藏着一条非常反直觉的规律：

真正重要的基础设施，是以数十年为单位做"预埋"的。

Berners-Lee 当年不知道谁会用 402——他只是认为"机器之间的小额支付总归会来"。他错估了时间尺度，但没错估逻辑。这意味着今天 Cloudflare 在做的"agent 钱包"、"stablecoin 结算"、"content pay-per-read"，不是创新，而是在偿还 1989 年留下的 IOU。

更出人意料的推论：这给我们一个方法论——判断一个基础设施是否长寿，看它预留了多少当前没人用的字段。HTTP 的 402 代码、IPv6 的巨大地址空间、Unicode 的保留区位——这些"冗余"不是浪费，是时间的赌注。反过来，今天任何以"刚够用"为设计原则的 agent 协议（MCP、A2A），都在为自己的早衰铺路。

四、隐藏的管理革命：Cloudflare 把员工管成了"token 代谢系统"

$300 收到提醒邮件、$500 通知经理、$1000 上报 VP——这个梯度看起来像费用管控，但它的真正身份是反向安灯系统（Reverse Andon Cord）。

传统丰田安灯：工人发现问题，拉绳子，停线。 Cloudflare 的反向版本：系统发现工人"用力过猛"，自动提醒。

这背后是一个未被明说的哲学颠覆：在 AI 原生组织里，稀缺资源不再是人的注意力，而是"对自身消耗的无意识"。员工不会主动意识到自己 10 分钟烧了 $50 token，就像人不会意识到自己每天眨了多少次眼。于是公司必须给每个人安装一个"代谢监测器"。

这与 Dane 说的"面试时发现候选人不在家里用 AI 是红旗"构成了一对完美的闭环：雇佣看的是你吸收新抽象的新陈代谢率，日常管理看的是你消耗新抽象的新陈代谢率。整个 HR 范式从"知识存量"切换到了"认知流量"。

一个让人意外的类比：这几乎是运动员训练的管理学——没人问短跑选手"你知道多少跑步知识"，大家只测你的 VO₂max、乳酸阈值、恢复速率。Cloudflare 实际上在把 5000 人的公司变成一支竞技代谢队伍，1000 个实习生就是源源不断的"年轻心肺"。

五、最反直觉的结论：安全不是会"修好"的，是会"相变"的

Dane 多次暗示"18 个月后一切会好起来"。但如果仔细听他讲的所有事——每周一个 log4j 级漏洞、70 年的软件要补、agent 不睡觉——会发现一个他可能自己都没意识到的推论：

我们不会"修完"旧漏洞然后回到安全态。我们会在修完之前，让"漏洞"这个概念本身发生相变。

类比：19 世纪末，城市因为马粪危机濒临瘫痪（纽约 1890 年预测 1930 年马粪会堆到三楼）。危机没被"解决"，而是被汽车让马粪变得无关紧要。

同理，当足够多代码由 agent 生成、由 agent 审计、由 agent 修复、由 agent 调用，"CVE 编号 + 人类补丁 + 季度扫描"这个范式本身会消失。取而代之的会是连续演化的、无版本号的、不可被人类完整审阅的软件生态——那时"安全"不再是一个二元属性，而是一个概率云。

这才是 Cloudflare CTO 真正没说出来的那句话：他不是在赢得一场战争，他是在赢得定义下一代互联网"信任"是什么的话语权。

Democratizing Security for the Agentic Web — Dane Knecht (Cloudflare CTO)

The AI Paradox: Both Cause and Cure

"AI has become the tool that's causing this kind of security apocalypse — it is also the tool that can help us solve it faster as well. It went from 'how do we get everyone using AI' to, all of a sudden, everyone's racing to figure out what AI security means."

"I've heard serious technical people say things like 'air gap everything important,' and 'we're not going to be able to trust the internet for a while,' and 'we just assume all the critical infrastructure and government services fall down at some point.' Is that your expectation for what happens?"

Opening: The Knecht/Connect Pun

Dane, I'm so excited to do this with you.

Yeah, thank you. Thanks for coming here, too.

I'm sure I'm not the first person to make this joke, but your last name — Knecht / connect. That's pretty good for the Cloudflare value prop.

Yeah. Yeah. There's been some jokes about renaming the show next year.

Cloudflare's Shifting Priorities

So with everything that Cloudflare is doing, what are your top few priorities as CTO right now?

Well, this past year it feels like 10 years compacted into one. So those priorities are constantly shifting, but it all goes back to our mission of helping build a better internet. That really hasn't changed over the last 15 years. We want to make sure the internet is secure, that everyone has access, that they can get their content online easily and scale it up.

Over the arc of the AI changes in the past year, it went from "how do you get everyone just to using AI, how do you make it easy for them to deploy and their agents to deploy," to — like most technical transitions — security being kind of an afterthought. And now all of a sudden everyone's racing to figure out what AI security means.

It means different things to different sides. One side, as a company, is: how do you keep your data safe from AI leaking the data out? But it's also: how do you keep people from getting in as well?

From Log4j-per-Year to Log4j-per-Week

Over the last 3 to 6 months, the number of vulnerabilities that are getting reported — CVEs — has just gone up exponentially.

Previously on the internet, we would see these Log4j moments, or Shellshock-type incidents, maybe once a year, and it would be all-hands-on-deck internally at Cloudflare to make sure we protect not just our enterprise customers but also all of our free customers — because we view it as a kind of public good and making sure the internet stays safe.

These things are now happening weekly. Not all of them are publicly reported on, but there are things as serious as the Log4j-type things, just happening at a greater frequency.

I expect that through the rest of this year, and in the next 18 months, the majority of teams' time is going to be spent on security. I think there was a stat put up earlier today during one of our keynotes, showing that over 50% of engineering time is going to start to be spent on security.

I don't think that will last forever. I think that will be a short transition — at some point AI will have surveyed the majority of the code and found most of the bugs, or found most of the shortcuts.

The Number Four: A Cryptographic Punchline

There's one that's kind of coming out today — has started to be blogged about and tweeted about — where one of the keys on the internet, that protects all TLS and WebPKI, which secures all your connections, was secured by the number four. Literally.

Basically, if you know about cryptography — it's all about randomness, right? That's why software has our lava lamps, so you can get good randomness. When a key out there uses the seed — the initial thing — to create it, with a single number four, it's going to be reverse-engineered.

AI can just do all these things. It doesn't sleep. It's not like the one engineer you had that was red-teaming things.

Last week I think OpenAI found the seeds for the NIST curves that were released back in 2000. These things are just moving so fast, and the bar is going up, and the models are just getting so good at cybersecurity. Midas was just the tip of the iceberg. And since then, it's not just been the models getting better — it's harnesses, it's how humans know how to use them, how to use those frontier models in order to find those exploits.

Who's Behind the Attacks: Enter the "Agent Kitties"

Given your visibility, what do you know about the humans behind these attacks and harnessing these models and taking the volume of vulnerability discovery up so quickly? Are they nation-state actors? Are they script kiddies? What can you say about how the attacker landscape has changed?

Well, I actually think for some of these larger vulnerabilities that have come out more recently, actually haven't been nation states. They've been high-school kids even — that are...

We're going to call them agent kitties now.

Yeah. Yeah. That are just spending their time — like they used to do capture-the-flag security contests. They're pointing their agents at an area and doing that. There's also financial award for them, whether it's bug bounties they get paid out — sizable amounts.

It's given the tools that honestly nation states have had in some forms for much longer — either through agents or just through the sheer number of people working on the problems — given to the masses.

Doomsday or Adaptable Humans?

This is the first time in 15 years I've heard serious technical people say things like, "Well, we should just air-gap everything important," and "we're not going to be able to trust the internet for a while," and "we just assume all the critical infrastructure and government services fall down at some point." Is that your expectation of what happens?

Humans — we are pretty adaptable, and we can move fast when we need to. I've seen the industry partner together when things like this happen. People that you usually think of as competitors are no longer competitors. We're just literally protecting critical infrastructure, as you said. When those critical moments happen, people will rise to that challenge.

So I'm a little less doomsday. I do think that a lot of the things we've done over the past 5 to 10 years — moving away from a kind of castle-remote infrastructure for security to more of a zero-trust approach — does put a lot of companies in a better position. You're not saying "this office is completely air-gapped." You're saying "these devices, these flows are secured in a different way." Everything's going to be tightened.

The 50% Security Shift

What is it going to take for organizations to do what you're describing? 50% of engineers do not work on security right now. I had Greg Brockman from OpenAI on the No Priors podcast last week, and he said that he thought in 2027 people were going to spend as much money on tokens for security as engineering. Very related idea — what is going to drive that shift?

Emergency. You're going to move forward all your security spend over the next 18 months — both from the red-team side (more offensive, actively trying to exploit things) as well as the defensive side (how you prepare things).

But I don't think that's going to last forever. I see a world in 18 months where new software productivity goes way up because all those resources are back focused on that. But there's definitely this period where security needs to be on everybody's mind.

Patching 70 Years of Software

What are some of the key elements of getting to a better place in terms of overall software and internet security? People discover of course that there are libraries and services everyone uses that had vulnerabilities that took effort to discover, and now do not. But part of my concern is that the rate of software production is also going up a great deal. So to some degree, we've got to go patch everything we have already made, and then keep up and get ahead of the pace of delivery.

Yeah. Well, for one — right now we are patching 70 years of software out there. So some of it is just catch-up.

On a go-forward basis, I think the software development lifecycle — the agent development lifecycle — is going to need to change. Luckily, the same way we can use security right now for red-team and things like that, it'll just be built into the process every step of the way. Software will just get more secure over time.

Reducing the Attack Surface

What have you learned about building secure production software internally already? There are many theories of how to do this — including broader use of formal verification, using agents for security in the development process. What do you think is going to create better software from first delivery?

I kind of go back to first principles there: you want to reduce your attack surface area. The easiest thing you can do is give fewer places for there to be vulnerabilities. So look at all your software and say: how can I simplify this? How can I reduce the footprint, the code?

Beyond that — formal verification, safer programming languages, things built into the runtimes that make everything safer will come. But it starts with... AI, at least for the early AI, is very verbose. It likes to create complexity. So AI, in the sense of what we've been dealing with, has actually not been helping build more secure stuff right now. But I think we'll get there.

That's where humans still come in — human judgment comes in — making sure that we design the software in a way that can stand on its own securely.

That was actually going to be my reaction when you say "reduce the surface area." I'm like, "Oh yes, of course, in principle." And that's not the natural inclination of today's models, right? I ask it to do something, and I'm like, "Well, like with one-tenth the complexity, please try again." Is that the role of engineering and security engineering today? Is that something that's going to be solved at the model level?

The way that humans did before agents, it needs to be solved at all levels. You need to train the engineers who are writing the code, the product engineers. The security teams still need to be involved in making sure there are checks and balances, a second set of eyes. You need to build in processes.

The Cloudflare "Codex" and Ten Commandments

We've gone to defining things a lot more internally on how we build at Cloudflare. Writing down our principles. We have a document called the Codex, which is like a bunch of RFCs the teams have built — here's how you build secure software at Cloudflare, here's how you build available software at Cloudflare, here's our best practices. And then it kind of gets boiled up into some "ten commandments" that the agents know how to follow and use at every part of the review process to help enforce those things.

You have agents out there writing a lot of the slop, and then deeper down in the factory, you have people doing the performance runs and the security runs. Just like how the company operated before, I think you need those adversarial reviews.

The "Messy Middle": Humans and Agents on the Same Rails

When you zoom out a little and look at overall traffic on the internet — how much of it has become agent-driven over the last year — I think it's outpaced most people's expectations. What has updated in your worldview of what the web a year from now looks like, either from an economic-model perspective or a security or requisite-infrastructure perspective?

I kind of think of it as: we're in the messy middle right now, where humans and agents are riding the same rails on the internet. Agents are trying to parse a human web — one, that's just inefficient. The web was designed for humans that could do things at different speeds: going to a website, being able to read and see the ads and participate in the fuller economic model, versus an agent that now can go to a thousand web pages in the same period of time. Which is great. It's just that you need to find a new economic model to support that.

Parallel Webs? AEO and the API Problem

Can we get parallel webs? Is there like a human web and a machine web? Everybody's trying to do — what is it called — AEO now?

Yes, I think we do. I think we find ways to deliver the content and meet agents and humans where they are, as opposed to trying to meet them in the same place.

Right now there are translation layers — a lot of companies that help an agent view a web page. These are all extra burning of tokens for things that probably don't need to happen. The website usually knows what data it has, and we've had things like this called APIs — ways computers talk to each other for years. It's just that APIs only covered a small fraction of the information on the internet.

Agents have a thirst to understand everything, and so they're going out and trying to explore the human internet. We need to make it easier for them. We need to make it less costly for the site owners, and we need to find a way for them to get compensated.

HTTP 402 Returns: Micropayments and x402

In a world where it can get very simple — most content websites, like a Substack, they know what their CPM is, how much money they should be making on ads for that site. So if an agent's reading that site, there is a world where an agent can decide whether or not they want to read the content, and then they can decide if they want to pay the CPM rate, right?

That's where you need new payment rails for the internet, that can do millions of transactions a second for all these little micropayments. All these things we've been talking about for years — micropayments always are "two years away" — I think agents will push that forward. And actually, I think we will see a world where there is a new economic model for content creators.

Who do you think the players are, or what are the variations of that infrastructure? I think obviously Cloudflare has an important role to play, but the rise of personal agents like Instinct and Muse has also made this an immediate question from a transactional perspective.

I don't think everyone knows, on the other side, what the business outcome is going to look like. Everyone's been through these transformations where the internet was going to kill Main Street — it didn't kill Main Street. Small business are still thriving. But there were people that were displaced, and so there's always some skepticism, and some natural inclination to just block them out — you saw Amazon just say "no personal shopping there, from an agent."

These are all people in that messy middle, trying to figure out what the path forward is and trying to keep some of their negotiation leverage. I think we will get to a place where Muse and Dots and all those personal agents will be able to accomplish tasks seamlessly, as a human could do, even easier. But I don't know if the technology is quite caught up to that yet — and the business models either.

Cloudflare's New Rails: Monetization Gateway, Wallets, Stablecoins

Is there anything you're personally excited about on the roadmap, or from a technical exploration perspective on the Cloudflare front, that you feel is going to enable this ecosystem in the future?

Absolutely on the content side — we've released a content monetization gateway, where we make it easy for people to put their sites behind us and take microtransactions for their content. Including providing wallets for agents to use, and a stablecoin that's going to help facilitate that transaction.

We're also doing things with OpenAI — a project called Signals — where we're making it easier for agents to actually discover content, instead of having to crawl the entire internet and continually go back to pages. We're making it easier for them to know what's new content, and more proactively do that. It's a win for the AI labs as well as a win for site owners not having to get constantly crawled and pay for that infrastructure.

So there's a whole set of new laws in the internet that I'm really excited to see grow. You know, x402 — when Stripe came out with it, I loved it, because it went back to the 402 HTTP code that Tim Berners-Lee created 20-plus, 30-plus years ago for payments. We kind of always knew that you needed better payment rails on the internet, but we haven't been able to figure it out. I think agents will lead us to that as well.

What Success Looks Like for a Content Creator

When you think about these initial products you've released — what would success for a content creator (or somebody who ostensibly had a website on the internet that they were monetizing with ads before) — what's the killer success case you guys need to see, or show the world, where it just becomes a default to do this?

Instead of them paying us, we're paying them, right? It's covering their infrastructure costs. It's providing money that supports their livelihood. We can actually increase the number of content creators out there — the last generation of the internet has done very well with YouTube and TikTok and X. I think we can actually make it exponentially larger.

Cloudflare OS: An AI Platform for Employees

When you look at the workspace OS-like release and ecosystem work you guys have been doing — what are you hoping are the biggest use cases of it coming up?

This is kind of transitioning a little — we released something called Cloudflare OS. It's our internal platform for how our employees use AI every day.

It actually goes back to security roots: we were very worried about customer data and internal data leaking out, and we wanted to make sure that our employees could use all the new AI tools and models, but have a way to safely deploy them internally — to understand how that data is being used and flowing, and have good governance over that.

The reason the company — the project — is called Cloudflare OS: we started to realize that as we had more and more agents, we needed to be able to teach them what made Cloudflare special, how we built Cloudflare. For humans we did that through Cloudflare University and the onboarding process and meeting your colleagues and working with them. But we needed to more clearly define that and document that for agents. So Cloudflare OS is both the platform where our employees can build anything they want in a secure way — without having to think about security; it's just built in there for them — but they also know that it's being done in a way consistent with the themes and values of how Cloudflare works.

Why Release It?

Why release it? I think of this as somewhat different from the other products Cloudflare offers today, in that it is not infrastructure — it's an end-user-facing product for managing AI use within the organization. Why release it, or do you think of it as a departure?

For one, it's kind of a reference architecture, really. Over the past 10 years we've built our developer platform — started with just a simple serverless compute primitive, and now over 100 different developer-platform tools, from storage to databases to Durable Objects. We wanted to show how you can build it completely on Cloudflare — how we build things internally — and give people the option to fork it and build their own version of their own company OS on top of it.

Who Benefits Most Inside Cloudflare

What is a way in which it is helping your people and your organization that you think is a clear success?

It's actually used more by our go-to-market teams and our G&A teams than it is even used by our engineering teams. Early on I thought training was the biggest gap for people using AI, and when you just point them at a chat interface or another vibe-coding tool, it's too much of a blank slate for them.

This is a platform where you design everything for how your business works, and they immediately can go there and get access to all the data they need. They can get guided and taken through where they quickly realize, "Oh, this is not trying to replace me. This is trying to make me better at my job." That's been really exciting to see — all the different ways people at the company have done that.

A lot of how this conference got put together — the marketing team built hundreds of internal tools. Previously they would have to go out and work with different agencies, but the speed they can move with a smaller team now is just amazing.

Restructuring to an AI-First Organization

Assuming this is a continuation of — starting in May you guys did this restructuring to be an AI-first organization — what else, reflecting on the last number of months, has worked or not worked that you would recommend to others?

The restructuring was hard. Saying goodbye to some of our colleagues was the first time Cloudflare ever did it. We had always been very careful not to over-hire. But this was for different reasons — because we saw the way AI was transforming some teams and how they work.

We kind of thought of it as a factory floor where you needed to actually rebuild, rethink how things happen. There were some processes — the way a product manager would send an email to customers. It involved three teams: - A BI team to get a cohort of the people you wanted to send an email to. - A marketing team to help design the email and get the voice right. - A marketing-operations team to actually get the email out.

You're never going to be able to redesign that process unless you make some hard changes and force people to rethink what actually is the right way to do that. It might not involve those three teams at all. It might just involve a new way of doing things.

What came out of that was a tool where a product manager now goes in and describes the cohort. They write an email, it rewrites it in Cloudflare's voice, it sends it to their manager — and the manager can click Approve if they like it, and it goes out. We didn't go from three teams getting faster at doing that. We went to one tool that can let a product manager now have a superpower that they didn't have before.

Who Owns Rethinking a Workflow?

When you think of all of the different workflows and tasks within an organization that's got about 5,000 people like Cloudflare, how do you decide who the owner is of rethinking that process? Was it bottoms-up from one of those teams in this case? Is it an organizational leader?

Cloudflare has always had a thousand more things that we could ever do, whether products, features, or things like this. We always look for people who are going to take initiative and ownership. It doesn't really matter if you're ordering them 1 to 100 and trying to prioritize them — any one of those hundred things is probably safe if someone's passionate about it.

At the beginning of last year we gave people the tools and started seeing how they were experimenting, and people quickly broke out into different cohorts — those who were really leaning in and naturally doing those things and taking ownership of them. It was very bottoms-up.

Token Budgeting: The $300 / $500 / $1,000 Ladder

It's been a major topic of conversation for organizations: how should they think about token budgeting? What's a reasonable amount to spend? How do I think about this versus human capital? Who should get tokens, even within our organization? What is your philosophy on this now?

It's definitely changed. Each model kind of makes you rethink it as the cost dynamics change. In general... I think it's kind of silly that we're actually asking humans to decide which model to use for each task.

Like, it should be intelligently routed.

Exactly. Humans just aren't ever going to be good at that. But early on, you do it by brute force. You get people to experiment and say, "Hey, for the planning part, let's use the top frontier models. Once the plan's written out and agreed upon and iterated on, some of the open-source models can go do that. Then you go back and have one of the frontier models do the reviews and the red-teaming."

All that today is fairly manual. But as we start to learn and experiment, people will become intelligent — and over time there'll be more governance on that.

No Token Leaderboard

Cloudflare has been in a place where largely we've let people use the models and tools they see fit for the job. We don't have a token leaderboard. We don't encourage it. We encourage people to focus on the output — they're not graded on whether they used it, they're graded on what they've shipped and what they've built.

But we found that just giving people notices works. If you happen to use $300 a day, you just get an email: "Hey, did you know?" Because most of the time people didn't realize they were doing it. And they're like, "Oh, huh."

Then if it gets to $500, it goes to your manager. If it goes to $1,000, it goes to a VP in a day. But those things rarely happen, and usually people are actually happy to get those notices.

Still Early: The Intern Strategy

Where do you think you are in your overall evolution — if you take even just the current level of capabilities of models, assume no new development — of rethinking the way different things at Cloudflare are done, from go-to-market to engineering?

Oh, I think still so early. Cloudflare did something two years ago — we had about 200 interns. What we saw was those interns were really the first fully AI-native cohort. If you took AI away from them, I don't think they would be able to work.

Is that good?

I actually think it is. I think they know how to use the tools better than us. It's just like, if you took Google away from me over the last 10 years, how would I learn anything, right? That's just where they reached for first.

We actually saw the managers that had interns from that summer adopt AI faster. So this past summer, this past year, we decided we're going to hire a thousand interns.

So that's — for a 5,000-person company. Yes. Wow.

Yeah. Over the course of the year still.

It's just been amazing — the number of ideas that come from the interns. With AI, fewer people experiment faster, and so having more ideas, getting more people in there... Just seeing the way they use AI — they need to fill out a form, they reach for AI. I still find myself where I'm like, "Oh wait, I've just been doing this manually still." And then I'm like, "Oh wait, actually I should be using AI." I don't think that's natural for most of us yet. That will take time. We're still very early in our AI journey.

I love the mass-intern strategy. I run a very small partnership, and we always have an intern or two floating around a team of about a dozen for ideas and intern energy and all that. But we just converted one of our in-college interns to full-time — and had him drop out and everything. I think you're right that maybe the dial should be turned up on the amount of DNA that is really really native to these tools.

I think it's great for them as well. You see schools like Waterloo and Northeastern with these co-op programs — people who get that type of real work experience are some of our best employees many years in, and go on to do great things.

Not a Master Plan — A Bottoms-Up Metabolism

It is interesting (or encouraging) that instead of a master plan where we're going to map out every department and sub-department at Cloudflare and say "here are the key workflows we're going to re-engineer," it is instead a strategy of: assume people are rational about their tokens if given information about their usage; hire a bunch of interns; and assume high-agency people are going to shift those workflows to something more intelligent over time.

Yeah. And then brute-force and just try things. Early on we had an email alias — agents@cloudflare — back in January of this year. We just told people: if you're curious, "Can I use AI for this email in your jobs-to-be-done?" and that email would reply back with the Skill file.

For a while people thought it was all AI and automated. It was actually a bunch of interns helping people write Skill files. But that let us see — in a way that's not "going out and hiring a consulting firm to come out and catalog every single thing to be done" — it's people recognizing: hey, this seems harder than it needs to be. I wonder if an agent can help me here.

Hiring: Curiosity as a Red-Flag Detector

Is there anything else about the last year that's changed — beyond the intern level — like your hiring philosophy, and what you look for in people to bring on?

One of the biggest things we've always looked for is curiosity. If people aren't using AI at home in their personal life — that's a pretty big red flag. How can you not be embracing AI if you have a level of curiosity out there? So I think just doubling down on some of those key characteristics — drive and curiosity and empathy — plays even better for this next set of people.

Well, I am an alpha user of all products and technology forever. But I think the answer is like fear and skepticism, right? Implicit in this claim about curiosity — including in experimentation with frontier tools — is that that needs to be a core principle for people who work at Cloudflare.

A lot of things we're doing, we're inventing new ways of doing things. The scale we operate at — for the number of sites behind us, and the amount of free services we give away — is just not possible with off-the-shelf technology. So you need people who can come in and literally invent new things. That starts with curiosity.

Final Round: Attacking the 70-Year Backlog

I have a couple questions to close out, mainly about security — both how to do that in a new way at Cloudflare, and then how you think it's going to work in the broader ecosystem.

If half the engineering team is going to go work on security and just fix 70 years of vulnerabilities, how do you attack that problem internally — assuming that not all software is perfect, even amazing production internet-scale software?

Largely... today we have one red team. By the end of next year, we will probably have four or five red teams. Break people out into groups that are more adversarial and actively trying to find vulnerabilities.

Why is that the approach, instead of "oh, we're finally going to get our patching systems right, our processes right"?

Processes could always be better. We have a VEN process, we have a patching process. Are they perfect? No. But the best way I've found for those sorts of things to get better is: out of crisis comes those fixes. When the volumes get too big for the engineering team to do them using their normal processes — engineers are inherently lazy, in a good way — they will automate away those things as they realize there's no other way to do that.

So the focus needs to be on the discovery side. People will do the right thing and figure out how to patch it in a scalable way over time.

Shipping vs. Patching

Do you express a philosophy on prioritization of this versus shipping new features? Because it's not as if we didn't have a backlog of vulnerabilities in every large piece of software to go fix. It was just whether that was a priority for engineering teams previously.

You need to figure out how to do both. It might come at the expense of cost optimization or other things. But companies — if you're not shipping, you're dying — is how we think about it. So you need to be able to continue building and shipping new things, but you need to make sure you're doing it securely and patching and fixing bugs.

If we do it right, we actually will be able to do them both faster with AI. While AI has become the tool that's causing this security apocalypse to happen, it is also the tool that can help us solve it faster. It's on both sides of it.

Open vs. Closed Models in Cyber

Where do you fall in this debate on the role, good and bad, of open and closed models on the cyber front? The broad argument is: defensive and offensive cyber capabilities are parallel in the same model, despite safety and guardrails being built into them. You can't have open defensive models without them also being offensive. And then the concern around only having security capabilities in a set of frontier closed models is: how are you going to release them? You can't possibly get them out to the distributed set of actors that need to defend. Did I characterize that correctly?

Yeah. Over time it all has to be open — because everyone's going to get access to it anyways. That's how open source tends to work. The bad guys are going to find a way to get it. The top companies will have a way of getting it as well. So all you are doing is excluding a mass population that just doesn't have the access that it probably needs.

Democratizing Security for Everyone Else

Final question — because Cloudflare, very mission-oriented, carries the weight of some internet resilience on its back: what about all the people who can't afford to have four red teams, or never had a red team to begin with, that run important systems? How do they protect themselves?

I would say: put your sites behind Cloudflare. Put your infrastructure behind Cloudflare. Build on Cloudflare.

When these major vulnerabilities come out — like the React one last year — we don't just give it to our paid customers who have the advanced firewall and WAF capabilities. We give it to everyone. We view those kinds of things as part of the utility that we offer. Just like we want to provide performance for everyone — before Cloudflare started, there were probably 3,000 sites in the world that had a large-scale CDN to cache their stuff at the edge. Now there are hundreds of millions of sites that do.

Cloudflare has always viewed our goal as democratizing security and performance for everyone.

Awesome. Thanks so much for doing this, Dane — and you guys heard it first: we have the agent kitties and the vuln-apocalypse. Am I pronouncing that right?

Yeah.

Yeah. But it's resolvable. All right. Thanks so much, guys.

Thanks.

Find us on Twitter at @NoPriorsPod. Subscribe to our YouTube channel if you want to see our faces. Follow the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen — that way you get a new episode every week. And sign up for emails or find transcripts for every episode at no-priors.com.

item.description:
## 一、被忽略的真相：加密学从未假设攻击者是机器
Dane 轻描淡写提到的那个「用数字 4 作为随机种子」的笑话，其实是整个互联网信任模型的墓志铭。几十年来，密码学的"实用安全"并非建立在数学强度之上，而是建立在**攻击者的疲劳曲线**之上——没人有耐心逐一尝试几亿次愚蠢的密钥选择。换句话说，我们把人类红队工程师的"注意力稀缺"当作了防御的隐藏基石。
而 agent 不睡觉、不吃饭、不索要加班费。这不是"攻击能力的提升"，而是**防御前提的失效**。我们突然发现，整个 WebPKI、整个 TLS 生态，都在用一个暗含的假设跑了 25 年：攻击者会在某个时点选择放弃。这个假设刚刚、永久地、不可逆地错了。
一个让人意外的推论：这意味着**所有"足够难"的旧东西都要重新定义"足够"**——不仅是加密，还有 CAPTCHA、反欺诈的"冷却时间"设计、甚至司法程序里的"合理时间内"概念。只要文明的某一环节曾默认"没人闲到做这件事"，agent 都会把它击穿。
## 二、"Agent Kitties"：教会与印刷术的 2026 版重演
Dane 顺口说的"不是国家队，是高中生"几乎是采

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个让人意外的观察：这不是宏观故事，是流动性故事

10月的利率下跌＋科技股下跌＋价值股上涨，是9月的完美镜像。表面看，大家都在用"美债收益率变化"解释一切，但真正值得注意的是这个反向关系本身在翻转——而翻转是不解释任何东西的。

真正藏在底下的信号，是博主一笔带过的那条Jefferies数据：20日滚动净卖压回到了2025年3月、2024年2月关税危机级别。更关键的异常是债券的MOVE指数在收益率下跌时同步飙升——这就像股票上涨时VIX也上涨一样内部矛盾。这是一个经典的强制平仓（forced deleveraging）签名，不是宏观判断。类比2007年8月的"量化地震"：所有看似无关的策略同一天崩溃，不是因为它们突然都错了，而是因为它们挤在同一个pair trade的两端。所谓"庄家爆仓"的直觉是对的，但它不是关于AI的判断，而是关于杠杆结构的判断。 这意味着：等到爆仓公告见报那一天，往往就是底部附近。

跨领域连接：Vera Rubin其实是把丰田精益生产搬进了算力世界

GTC发布的真正革命不是芯片本身，而是交付→上线时间从4-5个月压缩到1个月。博主提到这意味着每提前一个月上线、按云业务单位经济学算就是30亿美元的收入前移。但更深一层的意思被忽略了——

这是算力产业的"JIT转型"。过去Nvidia卖的是零部件，客户要自己组装AI工厂；现在Nvidia直接卖"AI工厂"。这改变了整个供应链的瓶颈位置：瓶颈从"芯片供应"迁移到了"电力供应"。所以Bloom Energy的报表才这么关键——当芯片不再是瓶颈，谁能在一个月而非一年内把电力接上，谁就捕获了那3-10亿/月的时间租金。这解释了为什么BE的capex单季跳升18亿美元：这不是追需求，这是提前锁定下一个瓶颈的定价权。换句话说，速度本身正在变成一种可以直接货币化的商品——像物流业的"次日达"溢价，但在十亿美元量级。

更隐藏的真相：Meta的"克制"是整个AI估值辩论的黑天鹅

博主说小扎很克制，因为token成本还没降下来——这句话的分量比看起来大得多。市场现在在争论"AI是否泡沫"，所有空头（Ken Griffin、Citadel的立场）都在用当前的需求去匹配当前的capex。但Meta的MUSE只开到美国和加拿大，不是因为需求弱，而是因为单位成本高到不敢全球开闸。

这是一个经典的Jevons悖论预埋状态：19世纪煤炭效率提高后，煤炭消费不是下降而是爆炸式增长，因为低价解锁了海量此前被价格压抑的需求。token价格每降一个数量级，MUSE会从"一个国家的实验"变成"全球基础设施"。空头在用"看得见的需求"做分母，但分母本身正在被成本压抑——他们本质上是在用被钳制的变量去判断取消钳制后的世界。

最颠覆性的洞见：你的睡眠质量就是你的风险模型

博主反复讲"扛不住就砍到能睡着为止"——这听起来像心理学鸡汤，但其实是最严格的风险管理公式。

现代组合理论把风险定义为波动率σ，但这是外部变量。真正决定你能不能活到周期尽头的，是你的内部风险容忍度——而睡眠就是这个变量的实时物理读数。有意思的是：睡眠质量比任何回测、任何Sharpe比率都更准确地描述了你的实际效用函数。因为回测里的你是能承受50%回撤的；深夜三点刷盘的你，是真实的你。

跨领域连接：这与神经经济学家Damasio的"躯体标记假设"完全吻合——真正的理性决策不是无情绪的，而是情绪作为快速评估系统给出的信号。睡不着不是"心理问题"，而是你的身体已经计算出了你的意识还没算出的真实风险水平。所以博主那句"砍到能睡着"实际上是在说：把你的组合调整到你真实效用函数能承受的位置——这比任何Markowitz方差矩阵都更深刻。

一个博主自己没点破的联系

他说"P/E先跌是在杀未来EPS"，并列举了2022年半导体、2000年网络股的例子作为"P/E和EPS双杀"。但他漏了一个结构性发现：每次P/E先跌而EPS最终没跌的时点，都发生在产业采用曲线的早期（2025年3月关税危机、2023年SVB、2020年3月COVID）；每次P/E先跌且EPS后跌的时点，都发生在采用曲线接近饱和的晚期（2000年、2022年）。

那么现在的问题就不是"AI有没有泡沫"，而是AI采用曲线在哪个位置。博主提到Microsoft Copilot从15M→30M用户、Meta MUSE 40天破千万——这些是S曲线的拐点特征，不是饱和特征。这意味着从历史模式看，当前这波P/E杀跌极可能属于"假信号"类别——但真正的检验要等到2026年Q1-Q2的EPS数据。

板块分化：10月是9月的镜像

So we looked at QTT in the second half. The chip version dropped by 16% in October. So it's very strong in terms of volume. Because in October, it's been only a few days of trading. Two weeks more. Because you see, the price of must-have products has risen by 12% throughout October. So, from this year to now, the two units that have risen are still the chip units and the energy units. However, in May this year, I remember that the chip units rose by 110% at most. 二、价格、EPS与估值逻辑

价格先行，基本面必须跟上

And generally speaking, from the perspective of investment, generally speaking, I can understand that prices are the first to go. Whether it's up or down, we can understand it this way. When the price starts to rise, for example, when the P/E starts to rise, your EPS must follow up. If your EPS doesn't follow up, it's probably just a matter of time. Because the P/E of this category in a short time is mostly just an emotional value.

Part of it may be to set the future EPS increase, and part of it is to set the emotional value. When your emotional value is hard to maintain, when your emotional value is declining, your P/E will naturally bounce back. At this time, it must be established in the situation where your EPS cannot keep up.

Nvidia 2024年的案例

I think the best example is the trend of Invertar in 2023. Invertar once had a period of time, for example, in 2024. In July of 2024, do you remember the Carrier Trade? In Japan, the Carrier Trade caused the decline of Invertar. At that time, some of the chip components were also taken down. At that time, the decline of Invertar was relatively large.

In that period, I think Invertar probably had a record of I think the most likely time for the market to go up is 7 or 8 months, at least more than half a year. The chart for the past half year can be understood as the market from suspecting to using two-weeks to the middle of the market. to slowly go from doubt to believe. There is a process in between.

PE与EPS的匹配关系

So when the price goes too fast, when the P/E goes too fast, your P/E, your EPS must follow up. I gave this example before. If the price goes up by one times, under the situation where your basic face has not changed at all, then your valuation will be doubled. If you can stabilize your stock for a long time, that means your EPS, your basic profit must double. Normal companies can't double their profit per year. This is a reasonable expectation. You can't expect all your stocks to be from the price of the EPE.

From the perspective of investment, from the perspective of investment, it must be that the company you invest in is a profit in the future, or its profitability, or its profitability increase. So when the stock price starts to move forward, the stock price has doubled, the stock price has risen by 80%, you must expect that this company can keep up with the fundamentals. If it can't keep up, then naturally, at one point, its price will definitely go back to the stock price.

BE的例子

So I think For many companies, including the company I mentioned, BE, it is also a very good example. At the beginning, it must be PE first, and PE reached 200 or 300 times. But as the basic side pushes forward, you will find that suddenly its PE itself or its valuation itself is not that expensive.

So the market needs... This is why these labels without basic support, after they have grown, we basically see how they go up and down. This is because there is no basic support, no profit support. Without profit support, there is no EPS support. Without EPS support, most of the time, a lot of transactions are on the market's story line and emotional side. After these story lines and emotional sides disappear, you will find out in the market how to go, how to come, where to go, and where to go.

This means that in the middle of the whole process, there is no long-term long-only capital. After coming in, put the plate there, or there is no additional purchase plate. Because it doesn't have a solid support or a basic support. This is the underlying logic behind it. Why do we have to go back and forth between the labels? But with the basic support labels, when the market is now... The semiconductor is about to... The semiconductor is now in a state of no difference. Basically, whether you have a basic or no basic, it will all collapse at the same time.

When the market collapses at the same time, Many landmarks may have been raided. After being raided, I believe the market will slowly stabilize. Because in the short term, no matter what the situation is, whether it's an institutional explosion or a story line, when all these things are disbanded, the final price will stabilize on its basic level. It will be where it should be.

三、市场叙事的脆弱性

软件板块的"反理性"案例

So I believe the market will eventually... It's often said that the market is rational. Just like in the first half of this year, the market is The first month of the software is one year and a half. From February of 2025 to June of this year, it will be 16 months. One year and four months. Especially in the first half of this year, do you remember that every time Anthropic announced a new product, the software dropped? When it announced a new product, the software dropped.

Is that reasonable? If you think about it now, do you think it's reasonable? It's not. But when we were there, we thought it was reasonable. If the software didn't work, Anthropic could destroy all the software. OpenAFA might also drop. But you will find it reasonable at that time.

I remember many people were afraid at that time. They all went to see when the next Anthropic's new product release was going to be. I remember very clearly. At that time, I remember the time when I went back to the beginning, it was at that time. Everyone was going to see the release of a new product at Anthropic. When is the actual point? If I have a software warehouse that will release a new product that day, I have to pay attention to it. But you will find that this is already very unreasonable. This is not at all from a value investment perspective. This is from an attempt to I think I seem to grasp the logic of market trading and then try to anticipate that this logic line will continue. This logic line can make a line out.

So I think I seem to have found an edge on this story line in the market. There is an advantage there. Then I try to guess, I try to look at it. As long as you have it, because it must have given you a two or three times of a head start, you will find that the last two times, the function of Anthropia was released, and then the software fell. So the next time I think it will be released, I think the software will still fall. This is a very standard way to make a cash outflow.

What is the basis of this cash outflow? The basis is a cash outflow in the market. It's gone. It has nothing to do with the basic. Even the logic line will change immediately.

2022年vs现在：完全反向的逻辑

For example, recently, you will find that the fall in the US dollar interest rate and the gold price are not related. The US dollar interest rate fell in October and the gold price did not react. Or let's make the time line longer. The fall in the US dollar interest rate From this year to now, there are two logic lines that you can't understand at all.

From this year to now, the interest rate is rising, right? From YTC to now, interest rates have been rising since 2017, but today they are still rising, right? In the past 10 months, in 2022, the market told us that when interest rates fall, it is better than the technology stock, better than semiconductor. So when interest rates rise, the technology stock should fall, and so should the semiconductor. On the contrary, in 2022, the value stocks are strong.

But it's different now. Now, in the summer, you will find that the value stocks have become weaker. When it was on the rise, it was a rise with a rise in the semiconductor and then a rise in the interest rate. Then when the interest rate fell in October, the value of the stock was strong, and then the technology stock and the semiconductor were weak. That is a completely different logic from 2022.

If you follow this logic of 2022, you will not be able to understand the trend of the youth market at all. But this is a change in the market story line. And this story line change often starts from the results to rationalize the trend. But you rationalize this trend, this time you rationalize this trend, you will find that the next time you don't work or the market doesn't trade according to this logic, what should we do?

坚持自己的方法论
